A ZUPREME-2 result below the monotherapy figure, or a narrowed Phase 3, would take us the other way. Whatever the entry, this should be sized as a wide-distribution option, not as a value holding.
sop_fair_value: DKK 340 a share (base case), against a live price of DKK 306.30 - about 11% of upside, inside a very wide band running from roughly DKK 160 to DKK 635.
sop_breakdown:

- Net cash after the development bill: DKK 8.6bn, or DKK 125 a share. Verified net cash of about DKK 14.0bn at 30 June 2026 (DKK 14,457m of cash and securities less DKK 411m of debt), less roughly DKK 5.0bn of net funding consumed over the next five to six years as Zealand pays its 50% share of the petrelintide Phase 3 programme, partially offset by Roche and Boehringer milestones. This is the single most important judgement in the valuation. Gross net cash of about DKK 197 a share covers roughly two-thirds of the share price, but it is earmarked money, not distributable money - which is precisely why we set no structural downside floor on this name.
- Petrelintide, Zealand's half: DKK 9.0bn, or DKK 130 a share. Assumes a real but not dominant commercial outcome - roughly USD 4-5bn of peak franchise sales at a 50% probability of success, with the tolerability advantage earning a meaningful but not category-leading share.
- Survodutide royalty: DKK 2.9bn, or DKK 42 a share. A positive Phase 3 offset by a serious tolerability handicap; the liver-disease programme carries most of the value.

risk_reward: Poor to the base case, attractive only to the favorable case. From DKK 306.30 there is about DKK 146 of downside to the adverse case of DKK 160 against roughly DKK 34 of upside to the DKK 340 base - the wrong way round. Against the favorable case of DKK 635 the picture inverts, with about DKK 329 of upside for the same DKK 146 of downside. In plain terms: at today's price the shares are close to fairly valued on the central outcome, and the payoff is a wide option whose good tail does not resolve until Phase 3 data late in the decade. There is no structural price floor - the large cash balance is committed development funding, and biotechs burning cash routinely trade below net cash. Sizing should reflect an option, not a value holding.

interrogator_dossier:
# Forensic Dossier — Zealand Pharma A/S (ZEAL.CO)
**Interrogator pass, 7 September 2026 · Copenhagen listing, prices in Danish kroner (DKK) · live price DKK 306.30**

Zealand Pharma is a Danish peptide-drug developer whose whole investment case now rests on one
molecule — petrelintide, a once-weekly amylin analog for weight management, half-owned by Roche —
plus a royalty on Boehringer Ingelheim's survodutide and two small rare-disease programmes. Six
earnings calls from February 2025 through February 2026 are on the record, and, critically, the
events those calls were building toward have since happened. That makes this an unusually clean
forensic exercise: we can grade management's promises against the actual data.

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

**February 2025 — the ambition.** The story opens modestly. Zealand is "a key player in the growing
obesity market" with a "differentiated mid to late stage obesity pipeline." Three assets carry
roughly equal weight: petrelintide (wholly owned, seeking a partner), dapiglutide (a GLP-1/GLP-2
dual agonist entering a large Phase 2b), and survodutide (partnered with Boehringer Ingelheim).
Two rare-disease programmes sit alongside. Management is candid about needing capital and a
partner: the chief financial officer notes "9 billion Danish in the bank" and says partnership
discussions are "very focused" on petrelintide alone, deliberately not complicating them with
dapiglutide.

**May 2025 — the transformation.** The Roche alliance lands and the narrative changes register
completely. "Zealand has never been in a stronger position than we are today." The deal is
described as "historic and transformative" — 50/50 profit sharing in the United States and Europe,
shared strategic rights, Roche funding all commercial manufacturing, and a new asset (Roche's
CT-388) added to the pipeline. From this call onward, the company stops talking like a licensor and
starts talking like a co-owner of a franchise.

**August–November 2025 — consolidation and a hard cut.** The story narrows deliberately. In
November 2025 dapiglutide is paused outright, despite management calling it "probably the most
differentiated GLP-1 containing mid-stage development candidate." The stated reason is discipline:
the GLP-1 field has become "increasingly crowded, requiring even greater and clinically meaningful
differentiation for assets which would be launched in the 2030s." This is the single most
credible-sounding moment in the whole transcript set — a management team killing an asset it
plainly liked because the economics no longer worked.

**February 2026 — the promise, restated one last time.** Entering what management calls "the most
defining and catalyst-rich year in Zealand Pharma's history," the chief medical officer restates the
target one final time: "a successful outcome for us would be data that reinforces our confidence in
petrelintide's potential to achieve approximately 15% to 20% body weight reduction in longer-term
Phase 3 trials." Alongside it comes "Metabolic Frontier 2030" — five launches, more than ten
clinical programmes, a Boston research hub, artificial-intelligence-assisted discovery.

**The pivot inside the arc.** Running underneath is a quiet but continuous repositioning of what
success means. In February 2025 the pitch is efficacy plus tolerability — "the same degree of weight
loss as the GLP-1 receptor agonist, but with improved tolerability." By August 2025 it has become
"we have to move away from focusing on speed and magnitude of weight loss," and the target band
widens downward to "10% to 20%, which the vast majority desire." By November 2025: "we are not
seeking to deliver the highest possible weight loss with petrelintide." The goalposts were moved
before the ball was kicked. That is not deception — the strategic logic about real-world persistence
is genuinely defensible — but the sequencing matters, and it anticipated the result.

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

The headline financials here are almost entirely an accounting artifact and must be dismantled
before anything can be read from them.

| Management claim | The number in our data | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Zealand has never been in a stronger position … financially" (May 2025) | 2025 revenue DKK 9.21bn vs DKK 63m in 2024; net income DKK 6.46bn vs a DKK 1.08bn loss; earnings per share DKK 90.22 | **True but one-off.** The +14,599% revenue jump and the 70% net margin are the Roche upfront payment recognised in a single year. There is no recurring product revenue behind them. |
| Implied ongoing profitability | Trailing-twelve-month free cash flow **negative DKK 1.80bn**; latest-quarter earnings per share **down 48%** year over year; consensus forward earnings growth **−67%** | **The narrative is far richer than the run-rate.** The underlying business consumes roughly DKK 1.8bn of cash a year. |
| The screener's "P/FCF 3.4x" and "99.7% gross margin" | Both derived from the milestone year | **Meaningless.** A price-to-free-cash-flow multiple of 3.4 times on a company burning cash is a divide-by-a-windfall artifact, not a valuation signal. The same applies to the DKK 522.8 discounted-cash-flow "fair value" on the stock page: it extrapolates a one-time payment. |
| Return on equity −48.3%, return on invested capital −24.9% | Scan figures, backward-looking | **Stale but directionally honest.** They describe the pre-windfall research-stage business, which is what remains once the upfront is spent. |
| "We have secured enough capital to fund our journey towards profitability" (May 2025) | Cash and securities **DKK 14,457m** at 30 June 2026 against total debt of DKK 411m — net cash of roughly **DKK 14.0bn**, about DKK 197 per share, against a DKK 306 share price | **Verified and the strongest fact in the file.** Roughly two-thirds of the market price is covered by cash. |
| "We can easily fund Phase 2 … and progress initiation of Phase 3" (February 2025) | First-half 2026 revenue DKK 4,525m, net profit DKK 3,524m; full-year 2026 guidance of DKK 4.5bn collaboration revenue against DKK 2.7–3.3bn of operating expense | **Verified.** 2026 is self-funding. Note, though, that the full-year revenue guide is already booked in the first half — the second half carries expense with essentially no offsetting revenue. |
| "Confident in the best-in-class potential" of petrelintide; 15–20% weight loss | ZUPREME-1, reported 5 March 2026: **up to 10.7% mean body-weight reduction at week 42** versus 1.7% on placebo | **The central claim did not hold.** The result is roughly half the low end of the range management had repeated across four consecutive calls. |
| "Placebo-like tolerability" | Same release: **4.8%** discontinuation for adverse events versus **4.9%** on placebo; overall withdrawal 8.4% versus 13.6% on placebo; **no cases of vomiting** at the maximally effective dose | **Fully verified, and genuinely remarkable.** This half of the promise over-delivered. |
| Earnings-beat record | Beat in 5 of 7 quarters (71%) | Modest corroboration, but for a pre-commercial biotech an earnings "beat" is mostly the timing of milestone recognition, not operating skill. |

**The forensic summary in one line:** everything management said about tolerability was true and
everything it said about the size of the weight loss was not. The balance sheet is exactly as
advertised. The income statement is a mirage.

---

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rising through 2025, then abruptly disciplined.**

- *February 2025 — measured, slightly defensive.* The chief financial officer will not guide on cash
  runway: "you don't really guide on the runway anymore … there are a lot of moving pieces." On the
  US filing for glepaglutide she is bluntly negative: "we are quite certain that we need to do
  [another Phase 3]."
- *May 2025 — peak confidence.* "Zealand has never been in a stronger position than we are today."
  "We feel very confident around the best-in-class potential." "We feel very comfortable in the
  position that we are sitting in now."
- *August 2025 — confident but hedging the metric.* "We are not seeking to deliver the highest
  possible weight loss." The chief executive begins pre-framing the competitive set: "of course, as
  we have also said for a long time, because amylin is such an attractive category, we should expect
  to see more competition."
- *November 2025 — sober, and better for it.* The dapiglutide pause is delivered without spin, and
  the chief executive says plainly it "was not, as you can imagine, an easy decision since the
  molecule actually looks very strong."
- *February 2026 — confident again, with the target restated.* "The most defining and catalyst-rich
  year in Zealand Pharma's history."

There is no shift from offensive to defensive language — the investment posture stays expansionary
throughout, and after the March 2026 data the company added a USD 200m (DKK 1.3bn) buyback in May
2026, which is an offensive act, not a retreat. What is missing is any pre-data hedging of the
efficacy number specifically. Confidence in the tolerability claim was correctly calibrated;
confidence in the weight-loss claim was not.

**Rating: Stable-to-Rising in tone, but with one materially mis-calibrated claim.**

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

Zealand splits cleanly into two very different track records.

**Operational and timeline guidance: High reliability.** Nearly every dated commitment was met or
beaten.

| Guided | When promised | Delivered |
|---|---|---|
| ZUPREME-1 enrolment complete by end Q1 2025 | Feb 2025 | Announced complete in March 2025, "significantly faster than initially anticipated" |
| 28-week primary-endpoint visit completed | Aug 2025 | Confirmed late September 2025 |
| ZUPREME-1 42-week topline in the first half of 2026 | Aug and Nov 2025 | Delivered 5 March 2026 — early |
| Survodutide SYNCHRONIZE-1 Phase 3 in the first half of 2026 | Nov 2025 | Delivered 28 April 2026 |
| Petrelintide/CT-388 combination Phase 2 start in the first half of 2026 | May 2025 | On track per the August 2026 half-year report |
| Partnership for petrelintide | Feb 2025 | Roche alliance, May 2025 — and on materially better terms than a straight licence |

**Scientific and product-profile guidance: Low reliability on the single number that mattered.** The
"15% to 20%" target product profile was repeated in February, May, August and November 2025 and
again in February 2026. The trial produced 10.7%. Management can fairly argue the trial met its
primary endpoint, that the estimand and the 42-week timepoint are not directly comparable to a
Phase 3 result, and that the target was always framed as a Phase 3 aspiration. All true. But an
investor who sized a position on the repeated 15–20% framing was mis-set, and the market said so
immediately: the shares fell on the print, and by 19 June 2026 the stock had recorded what press
coverage called its two worst days on record.

**Sandbagging pattern: none.** If anything, the reverse — this team runs ahead of schedule and
optimistic on outcome.

**Overall reliability: Medium.** High on execution, low on the one scientific claim that carried the
valuation.

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Three questions recur across the calls, and analysts were right about all three.

**Tolerability versus efficacy — the question that decided the stock.** Ollie Burrow of Goldman Sachs
(May 2025) pressed on the amylin competitive set. Mohit Bansal of Wells Fargo (November 2025) asked
the sharpest question in the entire record: he noted that a competing amylin's tolerability *worsened*
from Phase 1 to Phase 2 and asked "what do you expect with petrelintide in terms of tolerability in
Phase II trial as you see data in more patients?" Management answered with enthusiasm rather than a
number — "we have a high level of excitement and high expectations." As it happened, tolerability
held beautifully; efficacy is what came in light. The analyst was probing the right seam and got the
wrong half of the answer.

**The dose-response plateau — asked, deflected, and vindicated.** Carsten Lønborg Madsen of Danske
Bank (August 2025) asked why doubling the dose from 4.8mg to 9mg produced no additional response in
men: "isn't it also a little bit concerning to you that you see maybe no additional response … when
doubling the dose?" Management deflected to sample size — "remember, a small data set" — and to the
observation that women lose 3–5% more weight on any intervention. Seven months later ZUPREME-1
topped out at 10.7%. The flat dose-response in the Phase 1b data was a genuine early warning, and
the answer given was a non-answer.

**Cash runway — asked repeatedly, never quantified.** Laura Hindley of Morgan Stanley (February
2025) asked directly what the cash position supports. The reply: "you don't really guide on the
runway anymore." The company has never restored runway guidance. With Zealand now committed to
funding half of a large Phase 3 programme, this is the disclosure gap that matters most and it is
still open.

**What analysts are not yet pressing on.** Nobody in these transcripts asks what happens to Zealand's
share of profits if obesity drug net pricing keeps compressing — an issue that shrinks the pie every
amylin will share. And nobody has yet asked management to reconcile "15 to 20%" with 10.7% on the
record, because the last transcript in the file predates the readout.

---

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **The headline efficacy target was missed by roughly half.** Repeated across five calls, delivered
at 10.7% versus 1.7% placebo on 5 March 2026.

🔴 **The success metric was redefined downward before the data arrived.** "The same degree of weight
loss as the GLP-1 receptor agonist" (February 2025) became "10% to 20%, which the vast majority
desire" (August 2025) became "we are not seeking to deliver the highest possible weight loss"
(November 2025). Defensible strategy, uncomfortable sequencing.

🔴 **A dose-response signal was flagged by an analyst and waved away** (August 2025), and the final
result was consistent with the analyst's concern.

🔴 **Cash-runway guidance was withdrawn in February 2025 and never reinstated**, precisely as the
company took on a 50% share of a Phase 3 obesity programme — among the most expensive undertakings
in drug development.

🔴 **The reported profitability is an accounting artifact.** Trailing-twelve-month free cash flow is
negative DKK 1.80bn. The screener's Piotroski score of 3 out of 9 — a nine-point financial-strength
checklist — is the more honest read of the operating business than the 70% net margin.

🔴 **Insider buying is absent** (insider buy ratio 0.00 in our scan) even after the shares fell to
roughly 22% of the way up their 52-week range. Managers have been exercising and transacting in
warrants through 2026, which is compensation, not conviction.

🟢 **Tolerability over-delivered against an explicit promise, and by a wide margin.** Adverse-event
discontinuation of 4.8% against 4.9% on placebo, with no vomiting at the most effective dose, is the
best-documented result in the file and the one that supports the entire strategic thesis about
real-world persistence.

🟢 **Roche re-committed with full data in hand.** On 29 April 2026 — after seeing the 10.7% — Roche
and Zealand announced Phase 3 initiation for the second half of 2026. A partner that has already paid
a substantial upfront and funds all commercial manufacturing choosing to proceed is a costly,
informative signal.

🟢 **A genuinely hard capital-allocation decision was made and explained.** Pausing dapiglutide
(November 2025) removed a liked asset from a crowded field. Few managements do this.

🟢 **The partnership economics are unusually good.** A 50/50 profit share with shared strategic
rights, plus Roche carrying all manufacturing and supply capital, is far better than the standard
royalty licence a company of Zealand's size normally accepts.

🟢 **Capital returned rather than diluted.** In May 2026, after the disappointing print, Zealand
launched a USD 200m (DKK 1.3bn) buyback — DKK 742m executed by 7 August 2026. A pre-commercial
biotech buying its own shares rather than issuing them is a rare and meaningful signal.

🟢 **The balance sheet is verified and enormous relative to the market value.** Cash and securities of
DKK 14,457m against DKK 411m of total debt at 30 June 2026, plus USD 100m received in August 2026
from Royalty Pharma for the rusfertide economic interest.

---

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

**The vocabulary of the target quietly inverted.** Watch the adjective attached to weight loss. In
February 2025 it is *magnitude* ("15% to 21% mean weight loss"). By November 2025 it is *acceptance*
("a therapy that patients can and will accept to stay on") and the chief executive coins the phrase
"end the weight loss Olympics." A company that expected a large efficacy number does not spend a
year teaching the market that the efficacy number does not matter.

**The competitive framing hardened call by call.** February 2025: rivals are "some years behind us"
with "a rather inconsistent data set." May 2025: "we should expect to see more competition." August
2025: "research and development activity in amylin-based treatments has increased significantly …
two years ago, we faced some skepticism about our approach." February 2026: management declines
entirely to discuss differentiation within the amylin class — "it is too early for us to share our
thoughts about the ultimate differentiation between the different amylin analogs" — and falls back
on a focus argument: "this will be the number 1, 2 and 3 focus for Zealand … others will have to
spend more time thinking about existing franchises." That is a real argument, but it is the argument
of a smaller player, not a leader.

**Rival data was used as de-risking, and that cuts both ways.** In August 2025 management cited
cagrilintide's Phase 3 tolerability as "a major derisking event for the petrelintide program … as
petrelintide shares both a very similar receptor profile and a structure based on the human amylin
backbone." Having argued that a competitor's data validates their molecule, they cannot easily argue
that a competitor's superior efficacy is irrelevant to it.

**New voices, and what they signal.** The 2025–26 hires read as a commercial and industrial
build-out, not a research rescue: a chief scientific officer from Eli Lilly (April 2025), a chief
development officer (August 2025), a head of investor relations from Vertex and Shire (April 2026),
and Camilla Sylvest — a former Novo Nordisk commercial executive — proposed to the board in May 2026
explicitly "to bring deep commercial expertise to the Board at a critical stage, as Zealand Pharma
advances towards establishing its commercial footprint." The company is staffing for a launch it
intends to co-run.

**Two capital signals point in opposite directions and both are informative.** Selling the rusfertide
royalty for USD 100m (12 August 2026) monetises a non-core asset at exactly the moment the balance
sheet needs no help — that is opportunistic, not distressed. Buying back stock while running a
Phase 3 programme is either genuine confidence or, less charitably, a management team that would
rather support the share price than restore runway guidance.

**The GIP restart is a tell.** In February 2026 Zealand revived a previously deprioritised GIP
analog, describing it as a combination component. Coming three months after dapiglutide was paused
for lack of differentiation, this signals a company that now sees its future in combinations built
around amylin rather than in any single stand-alone molecule.

---

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: PIVOTING.**

Zealand is not the company these transcripts opened with. It has gone from a broad, self-funded,
efficacy-led pipeline to a concentrated, partner-funded, tolerability-led franchise bet, and it is
recycling capital — pausing an asset, selling a royalty, buying back shares, building a Boston
research hub — rather than compounding an existing earnings base. That is a pivot, and by and large
a well-executed one.

**The single thing the director must weigh before sizing.** Roughly two-thirds of the DKK 306 share
price is covered by net cash of about DKK 197 per share. The market is therefore paying only about
DKK 110 per share — an enterprise value of roughly DKK 7.5bn, or about USD 1.2bn — for half of
petrelintide, a royalty on a Phase-3-positive survodutide, two rare-disease assets and the platform.
That is a strikingly low number. But the cash is not a floor and must not be treated as one: it is
the earmarked funding for Zealand's 50% share of a large Phase 3 obesity programme running into the
2030s, and the company has refused to guide on runway since February 2025. The director's real
question is not "is the enterprise cheap" — on the parts it plainly is — but "how much of that cash
survives the development bill, and is a 10.7% amylin still a winner when Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk
bring theirs?" Size to the second question, not the first.

**Economic moat: NARROW, and narrowing.** The moat type is intangible-asset — composition-of-matter
intellectual property on petrelintide, twenty-five years of proprietary peptide chemistry and
metabolic data, and the switching cost embedded in an integrated Roche alliance that would be
expensive for either party to unwind. It is real: Roche paid for it and re-committed to it with full
data. But it is narrow and getting narrower. The evidence in the financials supports this reading —
return on invested capital is negative at −24.9%, there is no durable earnings base to defend, and
the 99.7% gross margin and 70% net margin are milestone accounting rather than pricing power. The
qualitative evidence supports it too: management's own account across four calls describes a field
that went from sceptical of amylin to crowded with amylin, and by February 2026 it declined to claim
differentiation within its own class at all.

**Secular threat: MANAGEABLE, not terminal.** The structural force worth naming is reimbursement and
price compression in obesity — direct-to-consumer cash pricing and payer pressure are compressing net
prices per patient across the entire category, which shrinks the pie every amylin will share. That
is a real headwind to terminal value, but the category is growing fast enough from a base where, on
management's own repeated figure, only about 2% of eligible United States patients receive
pharmacotherapy, that compression is dilutive rather than destructive. The genuine threat to
Zealand's terminal value is competitive, not secular: two far better-capitalised rivals building
amylins of their own.

**Is the cheapness a fear-print or a value trap?** Neither cleanly. It is not a value trap, because
there is no shrinking base to be trapped in — the enterprise is cash plus optionality, and the
optionality is partner-validated. It is not a pure fear-print either, because the March 2026 result
was a genuine downgrade to the asset's expected value, not a sentiment wobble. It is best read as a
wide-distribution option, priced somewhere between its adverse and central outcomes, on a franchise
whose downside is cushioned by cash and whose upside depends on a scientific question that will not
be settled before Phase 3 data late in the decade.

Management credibility 3 of 5 · trajectory turning · a narrow but real moat · moat trend eroding · structural threat manageable.

bull_thesis:
The bull case is arithmetic before it is science. Zealand Pharma trades at DKK 306.30 on the Copenhagen exchange (quote taken 7 September 2026), for a market value of about DKK 21bn. Against that sits DKK 14,457m of cash and securities and only DKK 411m of total debt at 30 June 2026 - net cash of roughly DKK 14.0bn, or about DKK 197 a share, topped up in August 2026 by USD 100m received from Royalty Pharma for the rusfertide economic interest. The market is therefore paying roughly DKK 110 a share, an enterprise value (market value less net cash) of about DKK 7.5bn or USD 1.2bn, for everything the company actually owns.

What that USD 1.2bn buys is not a hope. It is half of petrelintide - a once-weekly amylin analog for weight management - under a 50/50 profit share with Roche in the United States and Europe, with tiered royalties elsewhere, with Roche funding all commercial manufacturing and supply. It is a royalty on Boehringer Ingelheim's survodutide, which on 28 April 2026 reported a positive Phase 3 result: 16.6% mean weight loss and up to 17.8kg lost at 76 weeks, with both weight-loss primary endpoints and the waist-circumference secondary endpoint met. It is two wholly owned rare-disease assets - glepaglutide for short bowel syndrome, in European regulatory review, and dasiglucagon for congenital hyperinsulinism, heading back to the United States regulator. And it is an early pipeline including ZP9830, a Kv1.3 channel blocker for immune-mediated inflammatory disease that cleared its first human study cleanly on 18 February 2026.

The scientific case rests on a distinction the market may be getting wrong. On 5 March 2026 the ZUPREME-1 Phase 2 trial delivered up to 10.7% mean body-weight reduction at week 42 against 1.7% on placebo. That is roughly half the 15-20% management had promised, and the shares fell. But the other half of the readout was extraordinary and is being undervalued: at the most effective dose there were no cases of vomiting, discontinuations for adverse events ran at 4.8% versus 4.9% on placebo, and total withdrawals were lower on drug (8.4%) than on placebo (13.6%). In a category where, on management's own figure from the February 2026 call, roughly half of patients who quit GLP-1 therapy cite stomach and bowel side effects as the reason, a drug people simply stay on has a commercial value that a weight-loss percentage does not capture. The June 2026 survodutide detail made the point in the cruellest possible way: nearly a fifth of patients left that trial because of gastrointestinal side effects, and Zealand's own shares fell more than 20% on the news. The problem petrelintide solves is the problem the entire category has.

The most informative fact in the file is that Roche looked at the 10.7% with full unblinded access and committed anyway. On 29 April 2026, eight weeks after the readout, the partners announced Phase 3 initiation in the second half of 2026. A partner who has already paid a large upfront, funds all manufacturing, and shares profits equally is the best-informed party in this debate, and it voted with capital.

Supporting evidence sits on both sides of the balance sheet. Management delivers on operational commitments with unusual reliability: enrolment ahead of schedule in March 2025, the 28-week milestone confirmed in September 2025, the 42-week readout delivered in the first half of 2026 as promised, and the survodutide Phase 3 on time. It made a hard, well-explained capital decision in pausing dapiglutide in November 2025 despite calling it the most differentiated mid-stage GLP-1 asset available. And in May 2026 - after the disappointing print - it launched a USD 200m (DKK 1.3bn) buyback rather than issuing stock, with DKK 742m executed by 7 August 2026. Pre-commercial biotechs almost never buy their own shares.

Finally, 2026 is self-funding. First-half revenue was DKK 4,525m for a net profit of DKK 3,524m, against full-year operating expense guidance of DKK 2.7-3.3bn. The company is spending nobody else's money to reach its next set of readouts.

Conditions the bull case requires: petrelintide must hold roughly 10-12% weight loss in Phase 3 with the Phase 2 tolerability intact; the market must genuinely reward persistence over peak weight loss; the petrelintide plus CT-388 combination must cover the segment that wants more weight loss; survodutide must find a durable niche in liver disease and cardiometabolic risk despite its tolerability handicap; and Zealand's half of the Phase 3 bill must not consume the cash pile faster than Roche milestones replace it.
bear_thesis:
The bear case is that this is an option, not a value stock, and the option just got cheaper for a reason.

Start with what the screener says and why almost none of it is usable. The 3.4 times price-to-free-cash-flow multiple, the 99.7% gross margin, the 70% net margin, the DKK 90.22 earnings per share and the +14,599% revenue growth are all one number wearing five costumes: the Roche upfront payment recognised in 2025. Strip it out and the record is four consecutive years of losses from 2021 to 2024 - DKK 1.02bn, DKK 966m, DKK 704m and DKK 1.08bn - on revenue that never exceeded DKK 343m. The trailing-twelve-month figures to 30 June 2026 tell the current truth: free cash flow of negative DKK 1.80bn, latest-quarter earnings per share down 48% year on year, and consensus forward earnings growth of −67%. Return on invested capital is −24.9%. The Piotroski score, a nine-point financial-strength checklist, reads 3 out of 9. There is no earnings base here to be cheap against, so the DKK 522.8 discounted-cash-flow value on the stock page - which extrapolates the windfall - should be discarded entirely.

The scientific problem is that the central promise was missed by roughly half. Management repeated a 15-20% weight-loss target product profile in February, May, August and November 2025, and again on 19 February 2026 - the chief medical officer said a successful outcome would be data reinforcing confidence in 'approximately 15% to 20% body weight reduction.' Fourteen days later the trial delivered 10.7%. This was not a subtle miss and the market did not treat it as one: coverage on 6 March 2026 described disappointing weight-loss results sending shares tumbling.

Worse, the goalposts were moved before the shot. In February 2025 the pitch was 'the same degree of weight loss as the GLP-1 receptor agonist, but with improved tolerability.' By August 2025 it had become 'we have to move away from focusing on speed and magnitude of weight loss' and the band had widened downward to 10-20%. By November 2025: 'we are not seeking to deliver the highest possible weight loss.' A management team that expected a strong efficacy number does not spend a year teaching investors that efficacy does not matter. And the warning was visible: at the August 2025 call, an analyst at Danske Bank asked why doubling the dose from 4.8mg to 9mg produced no additional response in men. The answer was a deflection to sample size. Seven months later the drug topped out at 10.7%.

The competitive position is the real terminal risk. Management's own transcripts chart it: in February 2025 rivals were 'some years behind us' with 'a rather inconsistent data set'; by August 2025, 'research and development activity in amylin-based treatments has increased significantly'; by February 2026 the chief executive declined to discuss differentiation within the amylin class at all - 'it is too early for us to share our thoughts' - and fell back on a focus argument: Zealand will care more because rivals must protect existing franchises. That is the argument of a smaller player. Zealand is competing against Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly, each with market values north of USD 1 trillion, each developing amylin programmes, each able to outspend the entire Danish company on a single trial. And management itself made the analytical trap: in August 2025 it argued that a competitor's Phase 3 tolerability data de-risked petrelintide because the molecules share a receptor profile and backbone. Having borrowed a rival's data as validation, it cannot now argue a rival's superior efficacy is irrelevant.

The cash is not the fortress it looks like. Zealand withdrew cash-runway guidance in February 2025 - 'you don't really guide on the runway anymore' - and has never restored it, at exactly the moment it took on 50% of a large Phase 3 obesity programme. Registrational obesity trials are among the most expensive undertakings in drug development; Zealand's half of a full Phase 3a plus Phase 3b programme running into the 2030s is plausibly DKK 8-12bn, and glepaglutide's own Phase 3, the Boston research hub, and a ten-programme early pipeline all draw on the same pot. Note too that full-year 2026 revenue guidance of DKK 4.5bn is essentially all booked in the first half; the second half carries expense against nothing. Cash that is fully committed to a development bill is not cash available to shareholders, and it is why burning biotechs routinely trade below their net cash. Buying back stock while refusing to guide on runway is, on the unkind reading, price support rather than confidence.

Secondary assets are thinner than they look. Survodutide's Phase 3 was positive but the 7-8 June 2026 detail showed nearly a fifth of patients discontinuing for gastrointestinal adverse events; it enters a crowded GLP-1 field late in the decade against Wegovy and Zepbound, where a Barclays note quoted at the time said safety and tolerability remain the key issue. Glepaglutide already required an additional Phase 3 after United States regulators asked for more evidence. Dasiglucagon has been blocked for years by a third-party manufacturing classification. Dapiglutide was paused. The rusfertide royalty was sold. The pipeline that once had breadth has been narrowed to one bet.

Finally, positioning offers no comfort. Our scan reads smart-money interest at 5 out of 100 and an insider buy ratio of 0.00, with the shares sitting only 22% of the way up their 52-week range and 13% below their 200-day average. Nobody with an information advantage is stepping in.

What would confirm the bear case: ZUPREME-2 in people with type 2 diabetes reading out below the monotherapy result; the Phase 3 monotherapy design being narrowed or delayed; a competing amylin posting materially better efficacy with comparable tolerability; or Zealand's cash falling below DKK 10bn without new milestone income.
consensus_delta:
Where we disagree with the market is narrower than it first appears, and it runs in both directions.

The market's clearest error is treating the reported financials as if they described a business. Screens and headlines pick up a 3.4 times price-to-free-cash-flow multiple, a 70% net margin, DKK 90.22 of earnings per share and revenue growth of +14,599%, and read a cheap profitable company. Every one of those figures is the Roche upfront payment recognised in 2025. The trailing-twelve-month figures to 30 June 2026 are the truth: free cash flow of negative DKK 1.80bn and forward earnings growth of −67%. Any model anchored on the DKK 522.8 discounted-cash-flow value on our own stock page is extrapolating a one-off. This cuts against the stock, not for it - the cheapness that draws a value screener here is not real.

Our genuine disagreement with the bearish consensus is about the cash and the partner. Since 5 March 2026 the street has re-underwritten this as a company whose lead asset came in at roughly half its promised efficacy, and the shares have fallen from a 52-week high of DKK 556 to DKK 306.30. That is a fair reaction to the science. What we think it under-weights is that the market now pays only about DKK 110 a share - roughly USD 1.2bn of enterprise value - for half of petrelintide plus a royalty on a Phase-3-positive survodutide plus two rare-disease assets, because about DKK 197 a share is covered by verified net cash. And it under-weights the single most informative event in the file: Roche saw the 10.7% unblinded and committed to Phase 3 anyway on 29 April 2026. The best-informed party, one that funds all commercial manufacturing and shares profits equally, did not walk.

Where we disagree with the bulls is on what the tolerability result is worth. The bull argument is that a drug people stay on beats a stronger drug they quit - and the June 2026 survodutide data, where nearly a fifth of patients discontinued for gastrointestinal side effects, made that argument vividly. But this is a hypothesis about prescriber and patient behaviour in the 2030s, not a demonstrated commercial fact, and it will not be tested until Phase 3. Management effectively conceded the efficacy race before running it, widening its own target from 'the same degree of weight loss as the GLP-1 receptor agonist' in February 2025 to 'we are not seeking to deliver the highest possible weight loss' by November 2025.

One assumption on the street we would flag as untested: analyst coverage remained broadly constructive after the March print - eight brokers were surveyed as moderately positive in early April 2026 - but we could find no dated, verifiable current price targets for the Copenhagen listing, and our data provider carries no target coverage for it. We therefore assert no consensus target figure. Investors should treat the absence of a verified target as an information gap, not as agreement with our numbers.

Net of all that: the market is close to right on this name today. Our base case of DKK 340 sits about 11% above the price. That is not an expectations arbitrage; it is a fairly priced option with a wide distribution.
forcing_function:
There is no fixed date and no contractual payout that would force a re-rating, and investors should not pretend otherwise. What exists is a sequence of company-guided events, each stated only to a half-year.

The most likely trigger inside twelve months is topline data from ZUPREME-2, the Phase 2 trial of petrelintide in people with overweight or obesity who also have type 2 diabetes, guided to the second half of 2026 and not yet reported as of 7 September 2026. This matters more than its size suggests. Management has argued since February 2025 that amylin agonism may deliver weight loss in people with diabetes comparable to the non-diabetes population - something GLP-1 therapies notably do not achieve. If that holds, it is a genuine differentiator that the March monotherapy result cannot supply, and it would arrive against a market that has stopped expecting good news from this company.

The second trigger is the disclosure of the Phase 3 monotherapy programme design and its initiation, also guided to the second half of 2026. Trial size, comparator choice, endpoints, and whether the programme includes the GLP-1-experienced population management mused about in August 2025 will tell investors how much conviction Roche actually has. A large, ambitious programme with head-to-head elements would say one thing; a narrow, defensive one would say another.

Beyond those, three lesser events sit in the same window: initiation of the ZYNERGY Phase 2 trial of petrelintide combined with Roche's CT-388, which is the company's answer to the segment that wants more weight loss; completion of the European regulatory review of glepaglutide for short bowel syndrome, which would deliver Zealand's first wholly owned approval and a revenue line that is not a milestone; and multiple-dose Phase 1a data for ZP9830 in immune-mediated inflammatory disease, which is the first real test of the Metabolic Frontier 2030 discovery claim.

A fourth possibility is structural rather than scientific. With about two-thirds of the share price covered by net cash, an enterprise value of roughly USD 1.2bn on a Roche-partnered franchise, and a management team already buying back stock, Zealand fits the profile that attracts an activist or a strategic approach. Nothing of the kind is visible today and we do not underwrite it - but it is the kind of situation from which such approaches emerge.

The near-term calendar item that is genuinely fixed is the third-quarter report, roughly 66 days out on the usual mid-November cadence. It is unlikely to move the shares by itself: revenue guidance for the full year was already booked in the first half, so the print will show expense against little revenue.
valley_of_death:
The next three to nine months contain more ways to lose than to win, and the pattern of the last six months should be taken seriously.

The accounting turns against the company immediately. Full-year 2026 collaboration revenue guidance is DKK 4.5bn and first-half revenue was DKK 4,525m - the entire year was booked by June. The second half therefore carries operating expense with essentially no offsetting revenue against full-year guidance of DKK 2.7-3.3bn, which means the third-quarter report (roughly 66 days out, on the usual mid-November cadence) and the full-year print will show a company back in loss. That is arithmetic, not deterioration, but headline-driven selling does not always distinguish.

Cash draws down on three fronts at once. The buyback had consumed DKK 742m of its DKK 1.3bn authorisation by 7 August 2026, with the balance still to spend. Second-half operating expense runs against no revenue. And the petrelintide Phase 3 programme starts in this window - a registrational obesity programme is among the most expensive undertakings in drug development, and Zealand carries half of it. The mitigating fact is that the company received USD 100m from Royalty Pharma in August 2026 for the rusfertide economic interest, and holds DKK 14,457m of cash and securities. There is no debt wall - total debt is DKK 411m and the solvency score in our scan is a comfortable 9.1. Liquidity is not the risk. Cash conversion into an uncertain scientific outcome is.

The binary risks are the real hazard. ZUPREME-2, the Phase 2 trial in people with overweight or obesity who also have type 2 diabetes, is guided to report in the second half of 2026 - so plausibly inside this window. Management has argued since February 2025 that amylin agonism may deliver weight loss in diabetes comparable to the non-diabetes population, which would be a genuine differentiator. A result below the 10.7% monotherapy figure would compound the March disappointment and remove the last near-term chance to reframe the story. Separately, the Phase 3 monotherapy design must be disclosed; a narrowed label, a smaller programme, or a slipped start would be read as Roche hedging. Presentations of the SYNCHRONIZE-2 and cardiovascular-outcomes survodutide data also land in this period, and the June 2026 experience shows exactly how the market treats tolerability detail on that asset.

Competitive headline risk is continuous and outside the company's control. Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly both have amylin programmes running; a strong competitor readout at any point would reprice Zealand without Zealand doing anything.

Finally, the market regime is unhelpful for this kind of name. Long yields near 5.24%, a two-year yield at its highest since January 2025, and a central bank that may still be tightening are a poor backdrop for long-duration assets whose cash flows arrive in the 2030s. The one genuine comfort is that Zealand needs no external capital - it is self-funding, which the current regime specifically rewards. And our own regime record carries a directly relevant caution: across 2026, clinical and regulatory crash names have overwhelmingly failed to recover above their pre-crash levels. That cohort is drawn from regulatory advisory-committee crashes rather than Phase 2 misses, so the analogy is imperfect - but the direction of the evidence is not encouraging for a fast recovery.
positioning_washout:
The forced-selling has already happened, which is the most useful thing about the setup.

Zealand went through two distinct liquidations in 2026. The first followed the 5 March ZUPREME-1 readout, when the efficacy shortfall against a repeatedly promised 15-20% target sent the shares lower. The second was sharper: on 8 June 2026 the shares fell more than 20% - reported as much as 26% intraday - when detailed survodutide data showed nearly one in five patients discontinuing for gastrointestinal side effects. Press coverage on 19 June characterised these as the company's two worst days on record. The stock has fallen from a 52-week high of DKK 556 to DKK 306.30 and sits only 22% of the way up its 52-week range, about 13% below its 200-day average, and close to the 50-day average of roughly DKK 307 - it has stopped falling but has not turned.

The shareholder base that leaves on this kind of news has largely left. This is a growth and specialist-biotech register, not a yield or passive one, so there is no dividend-cut mechanism to trigger further mechanical selling, no index-exclusion cliff in view, and no covenant or maturity that could force a sale - total debt is DKK 411m against DKK 14.5bn of cash and securities. A major-shareholder disclosure from Capital Group on 30 June 2026 shows large institutional money still engaged rather than gone.

Two flows work in the shares' favour. The company itself is a persistent buyer: the USD 200m (DKK 1.3bn) programme launched in May 2026 had executed DKK 742m by 7 August, leaving roughly DKK 550m of authorised buying still to come into a stock trading about 97,500 shares a day. And in August 2026 the company added USD 100m of cash from the Royalty Pharma transaction rather than raising equity. Note also that our screener's net-debt field is wrong for this name and would mislead a mechanical screen - the balance sheet shows net cash of roughly DKK 14.0bn.

The residual selling pressure that remains is discretionary, not mechanical: specialist funds that own this for petrelintide will re-underwrite on the ZUPREME-2 result and the Phase 3 design. That is a real risk, but it is an opinion-driven flow, not a forced one. Meanwhile our scan reads smart-money interest at 5 out of 100 and an insider buy ratio of 0.00 - nobody with an information advantage is stepping in either. The honest read is a washed-out but un-sponsored register: the sellers are done, the buyers have not arrived.
moderator_conclusion:
This is a good business at a fair price rather than a good business at a bargain, and the honest recommendation is to wait for a better entry.

Start with what is verified. At DKK 306.30 on the Copenhagen exchange (7 September 2026), Zealand carries about DKK 14.0bn of net cash - roughly DKK 197 a share, or about two-thirds of the share price - against DKK 411m of total debt. That leaves roughly DKK 110 a share, an enterprise value of about USD 1.2bn, covering half of petrelintide under a 50/50 profit share with Roche, a royalty on a Phase-3-positive survodutide, two rare-disease assets, and an early pipeline. For scale, Viking Therapeutics is valued at about USD 4.1bn for a wholly owned obesity programme it must fund alone. On the parts, Zealand is not expensive.

But the cheapness has a cause, and it is not sentiment. On 5 March 2026 petrelintide delivered up to 10.7% mean weight loss at 42 weeks against a target of 15-20% that management had repeated across five consecutive calls. That is a real downgrade to the asset's expected value, not a fear-print. And it was foreshadowed: management widened its own success criterion downward through 2025, and an analyst at Danske Bank flagged the flat dose-response in August 2025 and received a deflection.

Against that sits the strongest counter-evidence in the file. The other half of the readout over-delivered spectacularly - 4.8% discontinuation for adverse events versus 4.9% on placebo, with no vomiting at the most effective dose - and three months later, on 7-8 June 2026, the market watched Zealand's own shares fall more than 20% because nearly a fifth of survodutide patients quit that trial over stomach and bowel side effects. Tolerability is demonstrably the binding constraint in this category, and petrelintide is the cleanest molecule anyone has shown. Most importantly, Roche saw the 10.7% unblinded and committed to Phase 3 anyway on 29 April 2026. That is the best-informed party in the debate voting with capital.

Where does that leave the numbers? Our base case sums the parts to about DKK 340 a share, roughly 11% above the price, inside a band running from about DKK 160 to about DKK 635. The pivotal judgement is not the science - it is how much of the cash survives. That balance sheet is not a floor; it is earmarked funding for Zealand's half of a Phase 3 obesity programme running into the 2030s, and the company withdrew cash-runway guidance in February 2025 and has never restored it. Cash committed to a development bill is not cash available to shareholders, which is exactly why loss-making biotechs routinely trade below their net cash. We therefore set no structural downside floor on this name.

On the market backdrop: the current regime punishes anything that needs to raise external capital, and Zealand needs none - it is self-funding through 2026 and its outcome depends on nothing macro. That independence is a genuine merit in a tape entangled with rates, energy and AI capital spending. But the same regime record shows that names which crashed on clinical or regulatory news in 2026 have overwhelmingly not recovered above their pre-crash levels. The catalyst that mattered here has already fired and, in this book, that is neither a mark for nor against - it simply means the residual value case must stand on its own. It stands, but not tall enough at this price.

The forensic quality is mixed in a way that is worth stating plainly. Execution credibility is high: enrolment ahead of plan, every dated readout delivered on or ahead of schedule, a hard and well-explained decision to pause dapiglutide in November 2025, and a buyback rather than a share issue after bad news. Scientific credibility on the one claim that carried the valuation is low. The moat is narrow - real intellectual property and a genuinely favourable Roche alliance - but narrowing, as management's own transcripts chart a field going from sceptical of amylin to crowded with it, with two rivals each worth more than a trillion dollars building the same class. Price compression across obesity drugs is a real headwind to the size of the eventual pie, though the category is growing fast enough that it dilutes rather than destroys.

So: wait for the wash-out, and name the level. We would become buyers around DKK 230-250 - at or near the DKK 233.5 52-week low, which is roughly gross net cash per share plus a token for the pipeline. At DKK 245 the central case offers about 39% of upside against about 35% of downside, with the favourable case intact - a materially better trade than the roughly one-for-four the current price offers. The two developments that would change the call sooner are a strong ZUPREME-2 result in people with type 2 diabetes, which would give the story a differentiator the monotherapy data cannot supply, or a Phase 3 design more ambitious than the market expects. A ZUPREME-2 result below the monotherapy figure, or a narrowed Phase 3, would take us the other way. Whatever the entry, this should be sized as a wide-distribution option, not as a value holding.
sop_fair_value: DKK 340 a share (base case), against a live price of DKK 306.30 - about 11% of upside, inside a very wide band running from roughly DKK 160 to DKK 635.

Base case, on about 69.0m shares, totalling DKK 23.5bn or DKK 340 a share:

- Net cash after the development bill: DKK 8.6bn, or DKK 125 a share. Verified net cash of about DKK 14.0bn at 30 June 2026 (DKK 14,457m of cash and securities less DKK 411m of debt), less roughly DKK 5.0bn of net funding consumed over the next five to six years as Zealand pays its 50% share of the petrelintide Phase 3 programme, partially offset by Roche and Boehringer milestones. This is the single most important judgement in the valuation. Gross net cash of about DKK 197 a share covers roughly two-thirds of the share price, but it is earmarked money, not distributable money - which is precisely why we set no structural downside floor on this name.
- Petrelintide, Zealand's half: DKK 9.0bn, or DKK 130 a share. Assumes a real but not dominant commercial outcome - roughly USD 4-5bn of peak franchise sales at a 50% probability of success, with the tolerability advantage earning a meaningful but not category-leading share.
- Survodutide royalty: DKK 2.9bn, or DKK 42 a share. A positive Phase 3 offset by a serious tolerability handicap; the liver-disease programme carries most of the value.
- Rare disease, glepaglutide and dasiglucagon: DKK 2.0bn, or DKK 29 a share.
- Early pipeline, ZP9830 and the discovery platform: DKK 1.0bn, or DKK 14 a share.

Cross-check on the enterprise value. At DKK 306.30 the market pays about DKK 7.5bn (roughly USD 1.2bn) for everything except the cash. Our base case values those same operating parts at about DKK 14.9bn. The gap is real, but it is entirely explained by how much of the cash pile one assumes survives the Phase 3 bill - which is why the honest answer is a band, not a point.
risk_reward: Poor to the base case, attractive only to the favorable case. From DKK 306.30 there is about DKK 146 of downside to the adverse case of DKK 160 against roughly DKK 34 of upside to the DKK 340 base - the wrong way round. Against the favorable case of DKK 635 the picture inverts, with about DKK 329 of upside for the same DKK 146 of downside. In plain terms: at today's price the shares are close to fairly valued on the central outcome, and the payoff is a wide option whose good tail does not resolve until Phase 3 data late in the decade. There is no structural price floor - the large cash balance is committed development funding, and biotechs burning cash routinely trade below net cash. Sizing should reflect an option, not a value holding.
