interrogator_dossier:
# Forensic Dossier — Zealand Pharma A/S (ZEAL.CO)
**Interrogator pass, 7 September 2026 · Copenhagen listing, prices in Danish kroner (DKK) · live price DKK 306.30**

Zealand Pharma is a Danish peptide-drug developer whose whole investment case now rests on one
molecule — petrelintide, a once-weekly amylin analog for weight management, half-owned by Roche —
plus a royalty on Boehringer Ingelheim's survodutide and two small rare-disease programmes. Six
earnings calls from February 2025 through February 2026 are on the record, and, critically, the
events those calls were building toward have since happened. That makes this an unusually clean
forensic exercise: we can grade management's promises against the actual data.

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

**February 2025 — the ambition.** The story opens modestly. Zealand is "a key player in the growing
obesity market" with a "differentiated mid to late stage obesity pipeline." Three assets carry
roughly equal weight: petrelintide (wholly owned, seeking a partner), dapiglutide (a GLP-1/GLP-2
dual agonist entering a large Phase 2b), and survodutide (partnered with Boehringer Ingelheim).
Two rare-disease programmes sit alongside. Management is candid about needing capital and a
partner: the chief financial officer notes "9 billion Danish in the bank" and says partnership
discussions are "very focused" on petrelintide alone, deliberately not complicating them with
dapiglutide.

**May 2025 — the transformation.** The Roche alliance lands and the narrative changes register
completely. "Zealand has never been in a stronger position than we are today." The deal is
described as "historic and transformative" — 50/50 profit sharing in the United States and Europe,
shared strategic rights, Roche funding all commercial manufacturing, and a new asset (Roche's
CT-388) added to the pipeline. From this call onward, the company stops talking like a licensor and
starts talking like a co-owner of a franchise.

**August–November 2025 — consolidation and a hard cut.** The story narrows deliberately. In
November 2025 dapiglutide is paused outright, despite management calling it "probably the most
differentiated GLP-1 containing mid-stage development candidate." The stated reason is discipline:
the GLP-1 field has become "increasingly crowded, requiring even greater and clinically meaningful
differentiation for assets which would be launched in the 2030s." This is the single most
credible-sounding moment in the whole transcript set — a management team killing an asset it
plainly liked because the economics no longer worked.

**February 2026 — the promise, restated one last time.** Entering what management calls "the most
defining and catalyst-rich year in Zealand Pharma's history," the chief medical officer restates the
target one final time: "a successful outcome for us would be data that reinforces our confidence in
petrelintide's potential to achieve approximately 15% to 20% body weight reduction in longer-term
Phase 3 trials." Alongside it comes "Metabolic Frontier 2030" — five launches, more than ten
clinical programmes, a Boston research hub, artificial-intelligence-assisted discovery.

**The pivot inside the arc.** Running underneath is a quiet but continuous repositioning of what
success means. In February 2025 the pitch is efficacy plus tolerability — "the same degree of weight
loss as the GLP-1 receptor agonist, but with improved tolerability." By August 2025 it has become
"we have to move away from focusing on speed and magnitude of weight loss," and the target band
widens downward to "10% to 20%, which the vast majority desire." By November 2025: "we are not
seeking to deliver the highest possible weight loss with petrelintide." The goalposts were moved
before the ball was kicked. That is not deception — the strategic logic about real-world persistence
is genuinely defensible — but the sequencing matters, and it anticipated the result.

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

The headline financials here are almost entirely an accounting artifact and must be dismantled
before anything can be read from them.

| Management claim | The number in our data | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Zealand has never been in a stronger position … financially" (May 2025) | 2025 revenue DKK 9.21bn vs DKK 63m in 2024; net income DKK 6.46bn vs a DKK 1.08bn loss; earnings per share DKK 90.22 | **True but one-off.** The +14,599% revenue jump and the 70% net margin are the Roche upfront payment recognised in a single year. There is no recurring product revenue behind them. |
| Implied ongoing profitability | Trailing-twelve-month free cash flow **negative DKK 1.80bn**; latest-quarter earnings per share **down 48%** year over year; consensus forward earnings growth **−67%** | **The narrative is far richer than the run-rate.** The underlying business consumes roughly DKK 1.8bn of cash a year. |
| The screener's "P/FCF 3.4x" and "99.7% gross margin" | Both derived from the milestone year | **Meaningless.** A price-to-free-cash-flow multiple of 3.4 times on a company burning cash is a divide-by-a-windfall artifact, not a valuation signal. The same applies to the DKK 522.8 discounted-cash-flow "fair value" on the stock page: it extrapolates a one-time payment. |
| Return on equity −48.3%, return on invested capital −24.9% | Scan figures, backward-looking | **Stale but directionally honest.** They describe the pre-windfall research-stage business, which is what remains once the upfront is spent. |
| "We have secured enough capital to fund our journey towards profitability" (May 2025) | Cash and securities **DKK 14,457m** at 30 June 2026 against total debt of DKK 411m — net cash of roughly **DKK 14.0bn**, about DKK 197 per share, against a DKK 306 share price | **Verified and the strongest fact in the file.** Roughly two-thirds of the market price is covered by cash. |
| "We can easily fund Phase 2 … and progress initiation of Phase 3" (February 2025) | First-half 2026 revenue DKK 4,525m, net profit DKK 3,524m; full-year 2026 guidance of DKK 4.5bn collaboration revenue against DKK 2.7–3.3bn of operating expense | **Verified.** 2026 is self-funding. Note, though, that the full-year revenue guide is already booked in the first half — the second half carries expense with essentially no offsetting revenue. |
| "Confident in the best-in-class potential" of petrelintide; 15–20% weight loss | ZUPREME-1, reported 5 March 2026: **up to 10.7% mean body-weight reduction at week 42** versus 1.7% on placebo | **The central claim did not hold.** The result is roughly half the low end of the range management had repeated across four consecutive calls. |
| "Placebo-like tolerability" | Same release: **4.8%** discontinuation for adverse events versus **4.9%** on placebo; overall withdrawal 8.4% versus 13.6% on placebo; **no cases of vomiting** at the maximally effective dose | **Fully verified, and genuinely remarkable.** This half of the promise over-delivered. |
| Earnings-beat record | Beat in 5 of 7 quarters (71%) | Modest corroboration, but for a pre-commercial biotech an earnings "beat" is mostly the timing of milestone recognition, not operating skill. |

**The forensic summary in one line:** everything management said about tolerability was true and
everything it said about the size of the weight loss was not. The balance sheet is exactly as
advertised. The income statement is a mirage.

---

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rising through 2025, then abruptly disciplined.**

- *February 2025 — measured, slightly defensive.* The chief financial officer will not guide on cash
  runway: "you don't really guide on the runway anymore … there are a lot of moving pieces." On the
  US filing for glepaglutide she is bluntly negative: "we are quite certain that we need to do
  [another Phase 3]."
- *May 2025 — peak confidence.* "Zealand has never been in a stronger position than we are today."
  "We feel very confident around the best-in-class potential." "We feel very comfortable in the
  position that we are sitting in now."
- *August 2025 — confident but hedging the metric.* "We are not seeking to deliver the highest
  possible weight loss." The chief executive begins pre-framing the competitive set: "of course, as
  we have also said for a long time, because amylin is such an attractive category, we should expect
  to see more competition."
- *November 2025 — sober, and better for it.* The dapiglutide pause is delivered without spin, and
  the chief executive says plainly it "was not, as you can imagine, an easy decision since the
  molecule actually looks very strong."
- *February 2026 — confident again, with the target restated.* "The most defining and catalyst-rich
  year in Zealand Pharma's history."

There is no shift from offensive to defensive language — the investment posture stays expansionary
throughout, and after the March 2026 data the company added a USD 200m (DKK 1.3bn) buyback in May
2026, which is an offensive act, not a retreat. What is missing is any pre-data hedging of the
efficacy number specifically. Confidence in the tolerability claim was correctly calibrated;
confidence in the weight-loss claim was not.

**Rating: Stable-to-Rising in tone, but with one materially mis-calibrated claim.**

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

Zealand splits cleanly into two very different track records.

**Operational and timeline guidance: High reliability.** Nearly every dated commitment was met or
beaten.

| Guided | When promised | Delivered |
|---|---|---|
| ZUPREME-1 enrolment complete by end Q1 2025 | Feb 2025 | Announced complete in March 2025, "significantly faster than initially anticipated" |
| 28-week primary-endpoint visit completed | Aug 2025 | Confirmed late September 2025 |
| ZUPREME-1 42-week topline in the first half of 2026 | Aug and Nov 2025 | Delivered 5 March 2026 — early |
| Survodutide SYNCHRONIZE-1 Phase 3 in the first half of 2026 | Nov 2025 | Delivered 28 April 2026 |
| Petrelintide/CT-388 combination Phase 2 start in the first half of 2026 | May 2025 | On track per the August 2026 half-year report |
| Partnership for petrelintide | Feb 2025 | Roche alliance, May 2025 — and on materially better terms than a straight licence |

**Scientific and product-profile guidance: Low reliability on the single number that mattered.** The
"15% to 20%" target product profile was repeated in February, May, August and November 2025 and
again in February 2026. The trial produced 10.7%. Management can fairly argue the trial met its
primary endpoint, that the estimand and the 42-week timepoint are not directly comparable to a
Phase 3 result, and that the target was always framed as a Phase 3 aspiration. All true. But an
investor who sized a position on the repeated 15–20% framing was mis-set, and the market said so
immediately: the shares fell on the print, and by 19 June 2026 the stock had recorded what press
coverage called its two worst days on record.

**Sandbagging pattern: none.** If anything, the reverse — this team runs ahead of schedule and
optimistic on outcome.

**Overall reliability: Medium.** High on execution, low on the one scientific claim that carried the
valuation.

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Three questions recur across the calls, and analysts were right about all three.

**Tolerability versus efficacy — the question that decided the stock.** Ollie Burrow of Goldman Sachs
(May 2025) pressed on the amylin competitive set. Mohit Bansal of Wells Fargo (November 2025) asked
the sharpest question in the entire record: he noted that a competing amylin's tolerability *worsened*
from Phase 1 to Phase 2 and asked "what do you expect with petrelintide in terms of tolerability in
Phase II trial as you see data in more patients?" Management answered with enthusiasm rather than a
number — "we have a high level of excitement and high expectations." As it happened, tolerability
held beautifully; efficacy is what came in light. The analyst was probing the right seam and got the
wrong half of the answer.

**The dose-response plateau — asked, deflected, and vindicated.** Carsten Lønborg Madsen of Danske
Bank (August 2025) asked why doubling the dose from 4.8mg to 9mg produced no additional response in
men: "isn't it also a little bit concerning to you that you see maybe no additional response … when
doubling the dose?" Management deflected to sample size — "remember, a small data set" — and to the
observation that women lose 3–5% more weight on any intervention. Seven months later ZUPREME-1
topped out at 10.7%. The flat dose-response in the Phase 1b data was a genuine early warning, and
the answer given was a non-answer.

**Cash runway — asked repeatedly, never quantified.** Laura Hindley of Morgan Stanley (February
2025) asked directly what the cash position supports. The reply: "you don't really guide on the
runway anymore." The company has never restored runway guidance. With Zealand now committed to
funding half of a large Phase 3 programme, this is the disclosure gap that matters most and it is
still open.

**What analysts are not yet pressing on.** Nobody in these transcripts asks what happens to Zealand's
share of profits if obesity drug net pricing keeps compressing — an issue that shrinks the pie every
amylin will share. And nobody has yet asked management to reconcile "15 to 20%" with 10.7% on the
record, because the last transcript in the file predates the readout.

---

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **The headline efficacy target was missed by roughly half.** Repeated across five calls, delivered
at 10.7% versus 1.7% placebo on 5 March 2026.

🔴 **The success metric was redefined downward before the data arrived.** "The same degree of weight
loss as the GLP-1 receptor agonist" (February 2025) became "10% to 20%, which the vast majority
desire" (August 2025) became "we are not seeking to deliver the highest possible weight loss"
(November 2025). Defensible strategy, uncomfortable sequencing.

🔴 **A dose-response signal was flagged by an analyst and waved away** (August 2025), and the final
result was consistent with the analyst's concern.

🔴 **Cash-runway guidance was withdrawn in February 2025 and never reinstated**, precisely as the
company took on a 50% share of a Phase 3 obesity programme — among the most expensive undertakings
in drug development.

🔴 **The reported profitability is an accounting artifact.** Trailing-twelve-month free cash flow is
negative DKK 1.80bn. The screener's Piotroski score of 3 out of 9 — a nine-point financial-strength
checklist — is the more honest read of the operating business than the 70% net margin.

🔴 **Insider buying is absent** (insider buy ratio 0.00 in our scan) even after the shares fell to
roughly 22% of the way up their 52-week range. Managers have been exercising and transacting in
warrants through 2026, which is compensation, not conviction.

🟢 **Tolerability over-delivered against an explicit promise, and by a wide margin.** Adverse-event
discontinuation of 4.8% against 4.9% on placebo, with no vomiting at the most effective dose, is the
best-documented result in the file and the one that supports the entire strategic thesis about
real-world persistence.

🟢 **Roche re-committed with full data in hand.** On 29 April 2026 — after seeing the 10.7% — Roche
and Zealand announced Phase 3 initiation for the second half of 2026. A partner that has already paid
a substantial upfront and funds all commercial manufacturing choosing to proceed is a costly,
informative signal.

🟢 **A genuinely hard capital-allocation decision was made and explained.** Pausing dapiglutide
(November 2025) removed a liked asset from a crowded field. Few managements do this.

🟢 **The partnership economics are unusually good.** A 50/50 profit share with shared strategic
rights, plus Roche carrying all manufacturing and supply capital, is far better than the standard
royalty licence a company of Zealand's size normally accepts.

🟢 **Capital returned rather than diluted.** In May 2026, after the disappointing print, Zealand
launched a USD 200m (DKK 1.3bn) buyback — DKK 742m executed by 7 August 2026. A pre-commercial
biotech buying its own shares rather than issuing them is a rare and meaningful signal.

🟢 **The balance sheet is verified and enormous relative to the market value.** Cash and securities of
DKK 14,457m against DKK 411m of total debt at 30 June 2026, plus USD 100m received in August 2026
from Royalty Pharma for the rusfertide economic interest.

---

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

**The vocabulary of the target quietly inverted.** Watch the adjective attached to weight loss. In
February 2025 it is *magnitude* ("15% to 21% mean weight loss"). By November 2025 it is *acceptance*
("a therapy that patients can and will accept to stay on") and the chief executive coins the phrase
"end the weight loss Olympics." A company that expected a large efficacy number does not spend a
year teaching the market that the efficacy number does not matter.

**The competitive framing hardened call by call.** February 2025: rivals are "some years behind us"
with "a rather inconsistent data set." May 2025: "we should expect to see more competition." August
2025: "research and development activity in amylin-based treatments has increased significantly …
two years ago, we faced some skepticism about our approach." February 2026: management declines
entirely to discuss differentiation within the amylin class — "it is too early for us to share our
thoughts about the ultimate differentiation between the different amylin analogs" — and falls back
on a focus argument: "this will be the number 1, 2 and 3 focus for Zealand … others will have to
spend more time thinking about existing franchises." That is a real argument, but it is the argument
of a smaller player, not a leader.

**Rival data was used as de-risking, and that cuts both ways.** In August 2025 management cited
cagrilintide's Phase 3 tolerability as "a major derisking event for the petrelintide program … as
petrelintide shares both a very similar receptor profile and a structure based on the human amylin
backbone." Having argued that a competitor's data validates their molecule, they cannot easily argue
that a competitor's superior efficacy is irrelevant to it.

**New voices, and what they signal.** The 2025–26 hires read as a commercial and industrial
build-out, not a research rescue: a chief scientific officer from Eli Lilly (April 2025), a chief
development officer (August 2025), a head of investor relations from Vertex and Shire (April 2026),
and Camilla Sylvest — a former Novo Nordisk commercial executive — proposed to the board in May 2026
explicitly "to bring deep commercial expertise to the Board at a critical stage, as Zealand Pharma
advances towards establishing its commercial footprint." The company is staffing for a launch it
intends to co-run.

**Two capital signals point in opposite directions and both are informative.** Selling the rusfertide
royalty for USD 100m (12 August 2026) monetises a non-core asset at exactly the moment the balance
sheet needs no help — that is opportunistic, not distressed. Buying back stock while running a
Phase 3 programme is either genuine confidence or, less charitably, a management team that would
rather support the share price than restore runway guidance.

**The GIP restart is a tell.** In February 2026 Zealand revived a previously deprioritised GIP
analog, describing it as a combination component. Coming three months after dapiglutide was paused
for lack of differentiation, this signals a company that now sees its future in combinations built
around amylin rather than in any single stand-alone molecule.

---

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: PIVOTING.**

Zealand is not the company these transcripts opened with. It has gone from a broad, self-funded,
efficacy-led pipeline to a concentrated, partner-funded, tolerability-led franchise bet, and it is
recycling capital — pausing an asset, selling a royalty, buying back shares, building a Boston
research hub — rather than compounding an existing earnings base. That is a pivot, and by and large
a well-executed one.

**The single thing the director must weigh before sizing.** Roughly two-thirds of the DKK 306 share
price is covered by net cash of about DKK 197 per share. The market is therefore paying only about
DKK 110 per share — an enterprise value of roughly DKK 7.5bn, or about USD 1.2bn — for half of
petrelintide, a royalty on a Phase-3-positive survodutide, two rare-disease assets and the platform.
That is a strikingly low number. But the cash is not a floor and must not be treated as one: it is
the earmarked funding for Zealand's 50% share of a large Phase 3 obesity programme running into the
2030s, and the company has refused to guide on runway since February 2025. The director's real
question is not "is the enterprise cheap" — on the parts it plainly is — but "how much of that cash
survives the development bill, and is a 10.7% amylin still a winner when Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk
bring theirs?" Size to the second question, not the first.

**Economic moat: NARROW, and narrowing.** The moat type is intangible-asset — composition-of-matter
intellectual property on petrelintide, twenty-five years of proprietary peptide chemistry and
metabolic data, and the switching cost embedded in an integrated Roche alliance that would be
expensive for either party to unwind. It is real: Roche paid for it and re-committed to it with full
data. But it is narrow and getting narrower. The evidence in the financials supports this reading —
return on invested capital is negative at −24.9%, there is no durable earnings base to defend, and
the 99.7% gross margin and 70% net margin are milestone accounting rather than pricing power. The
qualitative evidence supports it too: management's own account across four calls describes a field
that went from sceptical of amylin to crowded with amylin, and by February 2026 it declined to claim
differentiation within its own class at all.

**Secular threat: MANAGEABLE, not terminal.** The structural force worth naming is reimbursement and
price compression in obesity — direct-to-consumer cash pricing and payer pressure are compressing net
prices per patient across the entire category, which shrinks the pie every amylin will share. That
is a real headwind to terminal value, but the category is growing fast enough from a base where, on
management's own repeated figure, only about 2% of eligible United States patients receive
pharmacotherapy, that compression is dilutive rather than destructive. The genuine threat to
Zealand's terminal value is competitive, not secular: two far better-capitalised rivals building
amylins of their own.

**Is the cheapness a fear-print or a value trap?** Neither cleanly. It is not a value trap, because
there is no shrinking base to be trapped in — the enterprise is cash plus optionality, and the
optionality is partner-validated. It is not a pure fear-print either, because the March 2026 result
was a genuine downgrade to the asset's expected value, not a sentiment wobble. It is best read as a
wide-distribution option, priced somewhere between its adverse and central outcomes, on a franchise
whose downside is cushioned by cash and whose upside depends on a scientific question that will not
be settled before Phase 3 data late in the decade.

Management credibility 3 of 5 · trajectory turning · a narrow but real moat · moat trend eroding · structural threat manageable.

bull_thesis:
The bull case is now mostly arithmetic. At DKK 233.80 (Copenhagen, 12 October 2026) Zealand's market value is about DKK 15.5bn on roughly 66.3m shares outstanding after the buyback completed on 5 October 2026. Against that sits net cash of about DKK 13.2bn - DKK 14,457m of cash and securities less DKK 411m of debt at 30 June 2026, less the roughly DKK 0.9bn of buyback spent after June, with the USD 100m Royalty Pharma payment of August 2026 broadly offsetting third-quarter spending. That is about DKK 199 a share, or roughly 85% of the share price. The market is paying about DKK 35 a share - an enterprise value (market value less net cash) of about DKK 2.3bn, or roughly USD 0.36bn - for everything Zealand owns.

What that buys has just been re-validated by the people with the most information. On 7 October 2026, with both Phase 2 datasets in hand, Roche committed to a three-trial Phase 3 programme of about 7,000 participants for petrelintide - in people with obesity, people with type 2 diabetes, and people with cardiovascular disease. A partner that has already paid a large upfront does not fund half of the most expensive kind of trial programme in medicine on a molecule it doubts. Zealand owns half of the United States and European profit, plus royalties elsewhere, with Roche carrying all commercial manufacturing.

The October diabetes data also corroborate a narrower claim management made in February 2025: that amylin may work about as well in people with diabetes as without, which GLP-1 drugs do not. A 9.2% weight loss at only 28 weeks in diabetes sits close to the 10.7% seen at 42 weeks in people without diabetes. And tolerability held a second time - 1.9% gastrointestinal discontinuation against 1.7% on placebo. In a market where most patients stop GLP-1 drugs within a year, a drug people can stay on has a real home in maintenance - keeping weight off after an initial loss - which is how William Blair now frames it (8 October 2026). Add the royalty on Boehringer's survodutide, now positive in two Phase 3 trials with the liver-disease programme still to come, two rare-disease assets (glepaglutide for short bowel syndrome in European review, dasiglucagon for congenital hyperinsulinism), a combination trial with Roche's enicepatide planned for the second half of 2026, and an early pipeline.

Finally, much of the latest fall is a sector-wide sell-off rather than Zealand-specific news: on 12 October 2026 Structure Therapeutics is at its 52-week low, about 42% below its 50-day average; Gubra is about 16% below; Viking about 14% below. When the whole obesity group de-rates, a name whose price is 85% cash is the one most likely to be mispriced. Conditions: the development bill stays near DKK 5-6bn net of milestones, Phase 3 confirms the tolerability profile at scale, and the maintenance market proves sizeable.
bear_thesis:
The bear case is that the cash is not a floor and the molecule keeps disappointing. Three readouts in seven months have each been 'positive but not enough': 10.7% weight loss at 42 weeks (5 March 2026) against a 15-20% target management repeated across five calls; survodutide's type-2-diabetes Phase 3 (1 October 2026) at 8.2-9.8% counting all randomised patients with about one in five stopping for gastrointestinal side effects; and petrelintide in diabetes (7 October 2026) at 9.2% with an HbA1c fall of only up to 0.65 points, which William Blair called underwhelming. The market sold each one.

The competitive problem is not new but it is getting sharper. Eli Lilly's eloralintide, an amylin of the same class, reported Phase 2 weight loss of up to about 20% at 48 weeks in November 2025 with tolerability similar to placebo at its lower doses, and entered Phase 3 around the end of 2025 - roughly a year ahead of petrelintide, including a diabetes trial. Novo Nordisk's cagrilintide, inside CagriSema, is further ahead still. Petrelintide's one differentiator, tolerability, is matched by a rival with about double the efficacy and a trillion-dollar balance sheet. A 'maintenance' positioning is a smaller and more price-sensitive market than first-line weight loss, and obesity net prices are already compressing.

Meanwhile the cash is committed. The trailing-twelve-month free cash flow to 30 June 2026 is negative DKK 1.80bn; consensus forward earnings growth is about -66%; return on invested capital is -24.9%; the Piotroski financial-strength score is 3 of 9. Full-year 2026 revenue guidance was booked in the first half, so the second half and 2027 carry costs with little revenue. Zealand now pays half of a roughly 7,000-participant Phase 3 programme, a Boston build-out and its own rare-disease work, and has given no cash-runway guidance since February 2025. If net spending reaches DKK 8bn before petrelintide earns anything, about half of the roughly DKK 16.45bn of net cash and receivables is gone - leaving about DKK 127 a share of cash - and the operating assets are worth little; even then the adverse case is about DKK 190 a share, roughly 19% below today's price. The screener's 2.6x price-to-free-cash-flow multiple and DKK 522.8 discounted-cash-flow value are milestone artifacts and should be ignored. What would confirm the bear: a larger-than-expected development bill in the third-quarter report or 2027 guidance, a weak combination signal, or further rival amylin data widening the efficacy gap.
consensus_delta: Where we disagree with the market is now mostly about the cash, not the science. On the science we agree with the street: petrelintide is a very well-tolerated, roughly 10% weight-loss amylin, not the 15-20% best-in-class drug management promised, and William Blair's 8 October 2026 note - weight loss 'intriguing', blood sugar underwhelming, few meaningful catalysts within a year, likely used mainly for maintenance - is fair. One reported price-target cut, from DKK 400 to DKK 300 on lower peak-sales assumptions for petrelintide and survodutide, points the same way; we could not pin its exact date, and FMP has no target coverage for this listing. Where we disagree: at DKK 233.80 the market is paying about DKK 35 a share above net cash - roughly USD 0.36bn of enterprise value - for half of a drug Roche has just committed to a 7,000-participant Phase 3, a royalty on a twice-Phase-3-positive survodutide, two rare-disease assets and a platform. Even after charging a DKK 5.5bn development bill, our base case values those parts at about DKK 7bn net, against DKK 2.3bn priced. The market is either assuming a development bill near our adverse DKK 8bn with little to show for it, or it is selling the whole obesity group and not distinguishing a name that is 85% cash. We also disagree with our own screener: the 2.6x price-to-free-cash-flow multiple, the 70% net margin and the DKK 522.8 discounted-cash-flow value are all the 2025 Roche upfront payment and say nothing about value.
forcing_function: There is no fixed-date, contractual event that forces a re-rating. The re-rating, if it comes, is the market recognising that it is paying almost nothing above cash for partner-funded late-stage assets. Near-term markers, none with a fixed date or payout: the third-quarter report (expected mid-November 2026), which should give the first post-Phase-3-start view of spending; the start of the Phase 2 combination with Roche's enicepatide (guided to the second half of 2026); Boehringer's survodutide liver-disease and cardiovascular-outcome data; and regulatory steps on glepaglutide in Europe and dasiglucagon in the United States. The decisive data - petrelintide Phase 3 - are years away. This is a valuation case, not an event case, and we size it as one.
valley_of_death: The next three to nine months hold more ways to disappoint than to delight, but no way to break the company. The third-quarter report (expected mid-November 2026) will show a loss: full-year collaboration revenue guidance of DKK 4.5bn was booked in the first half, so the second half carries operating cost against almost no revenue. That is arithmetic, not deterioration, but headline sellers may not distinguish. More important is any first word on 2027 spending and Zealand's share of the Phase 3 bill - with runway guidance withdrawn since February 2025, a figure above our DKK 5.5bn base would push value toward the adverse case. There is no liquidity risk: total debt is DKK 411m against roughly DKK 13bn of cash and securities, and the solvency score in our scan is 7.5. There is no debt wall, no dividend to cut and no covenant. The risks are scientific and competitive: further amylin data from Lilly or Novo widening the efficacy gap, an early signal from the enicepatide combination that disappoints, or continued de-rating of the obesity group in a reflation backdrop that punishes long-dated cash flows. With the buyback finished on 5 October 2026, the company is no longer a buyer of its own shares.
positioning_washout: Most of the forced-selling pressure appears spent. Zealand's register is growth and specialist-biotech money, not yield or index money, so there is no dividend-cut or index-deletion mechanism to force further sales. Holders have now absorbed four disappointing prints in seven months - March, June, 1 October and 7 October 2026 - and the price sits at its 52-week low, about 21% below its 50-day average of DKK 295 and 28% below its 200-day average of DKK 323. Two cautions. First, the buyback that supported the shares since May 2026 completed on 5 October 2026, removing a steady buyer. Second, the latest leg coincided with a sector-wide sell-off across obesity names (Structure, Gubra, Viking), which can persist independently of Zealand's own news. We do not see mechanical, value-blind selling that would be worth waiting for.
moderator_conclusion:
Buy now.

At our last look on 7 September 2026, at DKK 306.30, Zealand was a reasonable business at about a fair price, and we chose to wait for a better one. The better price has arrived - DKK 233.80 on 12 October 2026, about 24% lower - but it came with news, so we lowered our fair value before deciding. Two readouts in the first week of October were each positive but underwhelming: Boehringer's survodutide in type 2 diabetes (1 October), with about one in five patients stopping for stomach side effects, and petrelintide in type 2 diabetes (7 October), with 9.2% weight loss at 28 weeks and a modest blood-sugar effect. We cut our base value for petrelintide and survodutide and raised the development bill, taking fair value from DKK 348 to DKK 305 a share.

Even at the lower value the shares now sit about 23% below it, clearing the 20% discount we require in today's reflation backdrop. The case is simple: net cash of roughly DKK 199 a share covers about 85% of the price, so the market pays about DKK 35 a share - roughly USD 0.36bn - for half of a drug Roche has just committed to a 7,000-participant Phase 3, a royalty on a twice-Phase-3-positive survodutide, two rare-disease assets and a platform. The thesis holds: the cash, the partner commitment and the tolerability are all confirmed by dated facts.

Be clear about what this is. It is an option on one molecule, cushioned by cash that will be spent - not a cash-backed floor. The payoff now leans our way: about DKK 71 up to fair value against about DKK 44 down to our adverse case of DKK 190, roughly 1.6 to 1, with further skew to the favorable case of DKK 565. That adverse case was raised from DKK 142 once it counted the roughly DKK 3.8bn of Roche milestone receivables on the 30 June 2026 balance sheet and the first rusfertide payment - even after a DKK 8bn development bill, about DKK 127 a share of cash remains. The moat is narrow and eroding - Lilly's eloralintide matches petrelintide's tolerability with roughly twice the weight loss and a year's head start - and the macro backdrop, which rewards cash flow now, is a headwind for a company with none. Part of the latest fall is a sector-wide sell-off in obesity names rather than Zealand news. Our conviction stays at a middling 3: the business is no better than in September, only cheaper. Size it as a modest position, and watch the third-quarter report in mid-November for the first read on Zealand's share of the Phase 3 bill - a figure well above DKK 5.5bn net would move us toward the adverse case.
sop_fair_value: DKK 305 a share (base case), against a live price of DKK 233.80, inside a wide band from about DKK 142 (adverse) to DKK 565 (favorable).
sop_breakdown: Base case on about 66.3m shares outstanding (after the buyback completed on 5 October 2026): DKK 20.2bn, about DKK 305 a share. (1) Net cash after the development bill: DKK 7.7bn (DKK 116 a share) - about DKK 13.2bn of net cash less DKK 5.5bn of net spend, raised from DKK 5.0bn at our last look because the Phase 3 programme confirmed on 7 October 2026 is large (three trials, about 7,000 participants) and Zealand pays half. This is the single most important judgement; it is why we set no structural floor. (2) Petrelintide, Zealand's half: DKK 7.5bn (DKK 113 a share), cut from DKK 9.0bn - the diabetes readout points to a maintenance-led, mid-efficacy product of roughly USD 3.5-4.5bn peak franchise sales at about a 50% probability of success. (3) Survodutide royalty: DKK 2.2bn (DKK 33 a share), cut from DKK 2.9bn after the 1 October 2026 diabetes Phase 3 repeated the tolerability handicap. (4) Rare disease: DKK 2.0bn (DKK 30 a share). (5) Early pipeline and platform: DKK 0.8bn (DKK 12 a share). Cross-check: at DKK 233.80 the market pays about DKK 2.3bn above net cash for parts we value at DKK 12.5bn before the development bill, or DKK 7.0bn after it.
risk_reward: From DKK 233.80 the base case of DKK 305 is about DKK 71 a share (about 30%) above the price and the adverse case of DKK 190 is about DKK 44 (about 19%) below it, a reward-to-risk of about 1.6 to 1, with further skew to the favorable case of DKK 565. The adverse case is higher than we first wrote because it now counts the roughly DKK 3.8bn of Roche milestone receivables on the 30 June 2026 balance sheet and the first rusfertide payment. There is still no structural floor - the cash is committed development funding, and cash-burning biotechs can trade below net cash. The pipeline computes the ratios from these levels.
peer_comps_note: The peer file lists Gubra, Viking, Structure Therapeutics, Ascendis, Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly and grades Zealand cheap against them; it correctly notes that the 2.6x price-to-free-cash-flow multiple is a milestone artifact. No live peer multiple override or anchor multiple was supplied, so we cite no peer multiple from memory, and earnings comparisons with Novo Nordisk (DKK 256.30, about DKK 1.14 trillion market value) or Eli Lilly (USD 1,182.67, about USD 1.11 trillion) are meaningless - they are commercial-stage competitors, not comparables. The useful lever is enterprise value against clinical-stage obesity peers, priced live on 12 October 2026: Viking Therapeutics carries a market value of about USD 3.3bn for a wholly owned obesity programme it must fund alone; Structure Therapeutics about USD 1.4bn; Gubra about DKK 4.7bn. Zealand's market value is about DKK 15.5bn (roughly USD 2.4bn), of which about USD 2.1bn is net cash, leaving roughly USD 0.36bn of enterprise value for half of a Phase-3 amylin, a Phase-3-positive royalty and two rare-disease assets. On that frame Zealand is cheap against its peers. Caution: the whole group fell together over September-October 2026 (Structure at its 52-week low, Gubra and Viking 14-16% below their 50-day averages), so part of the move is shared sector beta, not a Zealand-specific mispricing; we credit only the enterprise-value gap, not the price fall, as name-specific.
interrogator_dossier:
# Forensic Dossier - Zealand Pharma A/S (ZEAL.CO)
**Interrogator pass, 12 October 2026 · Copenhagen listing, prices in Danish kroner (DKK) · live price DKK 233.80 (FMP quote, 12 October 2026)**

Zealand Pharma is a Danish peptide-drug developer whose investment case rests on one molecule -
petrelintide, a once-weekly amylin analog for weight management, half-owned by Roche - plus a
royalty on Boehringer Ingelheim's survodutide and two small rare-disease programmes. The transcript
file holds five earnings calls, from February 2025 through 19 February 2026; the May and August 2026
calls are not in the file, so everything after February 2026 below comes from dated company
announcements and press coverage, not from management's own words on a call. Since our last full look
on 7 September 2026 the shares have fallen from DKK 306.30 to DKK 233.80, about 24%, and three dated
events landed inside that window: the survodutide type-2-diabetes Phase 3 presentation (1 October),
completion of the share buyback (5 October), and the petrelintide type-2-diabetes Phase 2 readout
together with the start of Phase 3 (7 October).

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

**February 2025 - the ambition.** Zealand presents itself as aiming to be "a key player in the
growing obesity market" with a "differentiated mid to late stage obesity pipeline." Three obesity
assets carry roughly equal weight - petrelintide (then wholly owned and seeking a partner),
dapiglutide, and survodutide - with two rare-disease programmes alongside. The chief financial
officer will not guide on cash runway.

**May 2025 - the transformation.** The Roche alliance lands: a 50/50 profit share in the United
States and Europe, Roche funding all commercial manufacturing, and Roche's CT-388 (now named
enicepatide) added as a combination partner. "Zealand has never been in a stronger position than we
are today." From here the company talks like a co-owner of a franchise rather than a licensor.

**August-November 2025 - narrowing, and a hard cut.** Dapiglutide is paused in November 2025
despite management calling it "probably the most differentiated GLP-1 containing mid-stage
development candidate," because the field had become "increasingly crowded." At the same time the
efficacy pitch is softened: from matching GLP-1 weight loss "with improved tolerability" (February
2025) to "10% to 20%, which the vast majority desire" (August 2025) to "we are not seeking to deliver
the highest possible weight loss" (November 2025).

**February 2026 - the promise restated.** The chief medical officer frames success as "data that
reinforces our confidence in petrelintide's potential to achieve approximately 15% to 20% body
weight reduction in longer-term Phase 3 trials," in what management calls "the most defining and
catalyst-rich year in Zealand Pharma's history."

**March-October 2026 - the data arrives, three times, each "positive but not enough."**
- 5 March 2026, ZUPREME-1: up to 10.7% mean weight loss at 42 weeks versus 1.7% on placebo, with
  placebo-like tolerability. The shares fell sharply.
- 28 April and 7-8 June 2026, survodutide (Boehringer): Phase 3 positive at 16.6% weight loss, but
  nearly one in five patients stopped for gastrointestinal side effects; the shares fell more than
  20% in June.
- 1 October 2026, survodutide SYNCHRONIZE-2 (people with obesity and type 2 diabetes), presented at
  the European diabetes congress and published in the New England Journal of Medicine: both primary
  endpoints met, up to 13.1% weight loss if patients stay on drug but 8.2-9.8% versus 3.9% on placebo
  counting everyone randomised, with gastrointestinal discontinuations again near 18%. Press reports
  the shares fell more than 8%.
- 7 October 2026, ZUPREME-2 (petrelintide in type 2 diabetes): primary endpoint met, 7.4-9.2% weight
  loss at 28 weeks versus 2.0% on placebo, a fall in HbA1c (a three-month average blood-sugar
  measure) of up to 0.65 points, and gastrointestinal discontinuation of 1.9% versus 1.7% on placebo.
  Roche and Zealand started a Phase 3 programme of three trials and about 7,000 participants. The
  shares fell a further 3-4% on 8 October; William Blair called the weight loss "intriguing" but was
  underwhelmed by the blood-sugar effect and saw few meaningful catalysts within a year.

The arc is now complete: a company that promised a best-in-class amylin has delivered a
best-tolerated, mid-efficacy amylin, and has repositioned it - as the analysts now describe it - for
the maintenance setting.

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

The headline financials are an accounting artifact and must be taken apart before anything is read
from them.

| Management claim | The number in our data | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Never been in a stronger position" (May 2025) | 2025 revenue DKK 9.21bn vs DKK 63m in 2024; net income DKK 6.46bn vs a DKK 1.08bn loss; earnings per share DKK 90.22 | **True but one-off.** The +14,599% revenue jump and 70% net margin are the Roche upfront payment recognised in one year. |
| Implied ongoing profitability | Trailing-twelve-month (TTM) free cash flow **negative DKK 1.80bn** to 30 June 2026; latest-quarter earnings per share **down 48%** year on year; consensus forward earnings growth **-66%** | **The run-rate is a cash-consuming research company.** |
| The scan's "P/FCF 2.6x" and the DKK 522.8 discounted-cash-flow value | Both built on the milestone year | **Meaningless.** A price-to-free-cash-flow multiple on a company burning cash is a divide-by-windfall artifact. |
| "We have secured enough capital to fund our journey towards profitability" | Cash and securities DKK 14,457m against total debt DKK 411m at 30 June 2026 (net cash about DKK 14.05bn); buyback finished 5 October 2026 at about DKK 1.3bn in total, leaving about 66.3m shares outstanding; USD 100m received from Royalty Pharma in August 2026 | **Verified, and now larger than ever relative to the price.** Net cash after the buyback is roughly DKK 13.2bn, about DKK 199 a share - about 85% of today's DKK 233.80. |
| "Confident in the best-in-class potential"; 15-20% weight loss | 10.7% at 42 weeks (March 2026); 9.2% at 28 weeks in type 2 diabetes (October 2026) | **Did not hold on magnitude.** The diabetes result does support a narrower claim management made in February 2025 - that amylin may work about as well in people with diabetes as without, unlike GLP-1 drugs - since 9.2% at 28 weeks in diabetes sits close to the non-diabetes curve. |
| "Placebo-like tolerability" | 4.8% vs 4.9% adverse-event discontinuation (March); 1.9% vs 1.7% gastrointestinal discontinuation (October) | **Verified twice.** The one claim that has fully held. |
| Beat rate | 5 of 7 quarters (71%) | Weak evidence: for a pre-commercial biotech a "beat" is mostly milestone timing. |

**One-line summary:** the balance sheet is exactly as advertised, the tolerability is exactly as
advertised, and the efficacy is not.

---

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rising through 2025, then disciplined; no transcript yet covers the post-data period.**

- February 2025 - measured: "you don't really guide on the runway anymore."
- May 2025 - peak confidence: "we feel very confident around the best-in-class potential."
- August 2025 - confident but hedging the metric: "we have to move away from focusing on speed and
  magnitude of weight loss."
- November 2025 - sober: the dapiglutide pause "was not, as you can imagine, an easy decision since
  the molecule actually looks very strong."
- February 2026 - confident again, with the 15-20% target restated.

Actions after the data have stayed offensive rather than defensive: a USD 200m (DKK 1.3bn) buyback
launched in May 2026 and completed early on 5 October 2026, and a 7,000-participant Phase 3 started
with Roche in October. **Rating: Stable in tone, with the efficacy claim mis-calibrated.**

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Timelines: High.** Every dated commitment we can check was met or beaten - ZUPREME-1 enrolment
(early), ZUPREME-1 topline (5 March 2026, inside "first half 2026"), ZUPREME-2 topline (7 October
2026, inside "second half 2026"), Phase 3 initiation (October 2026, inside "second half 2026"), and the
Roche partnership itself.

**Scientific profile: Low on the number that carried the valuation.** The 15-20% target was
repeated across five calls and the trials have produced 10.7% (42 weeks) and 9.2% (28 weeks, diabetes).

**Sandbagging: none - the reverse.** This team runs early on schedule and optimistic on outcome.

**Overall reliability: Medium.**

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- **Dose-response plateau** - Danske Bank's analyst asked in August 2025 why doubling the dose added
  no response in men; management pointed to "a small data set." Both 2026 readouts are consistent with
  a ceiling near 10%.
- **Tolerability durability** - Wells Fargo (November 2025) asked whether tolerability would worsen in
  bigger trials. It did not; this concern has been answered in Zealand's favour, twice.
- **Cash runway** - asked in February 2025 by Morgan Stanley and never quantified. It matters more now:
  Zealand pays half of a 7,000-participant Phase 3 programme.
- **What is not being asked on the record:** how petrelintide competes with Eli Lilly's eloralintide,
  an amylin of the same class that reported Phase 2 weight loss of up to about 20% at 48 weeks in
  November 2025 and moved into Phase 3 around year-end 2025, roughly a year ahead of petrelintide. No
  call in the file addresses it, because the last one predates the comparison becoming stark.

---

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **Efficacy missed the promised range, twice.** 10.7% (March 2026) and 9.2% in diabetes (October
2026) against a 15-20% target.

🔴 **The blood-sugar effect in diabetes is modest.** An HbA1c fall of up to 0.65 points at 28 weeks
is well short of what GLP-1-based drugs deliver, which limits petrelintide as a stand-alone diabetes
drug.

🔴 **The royalty asset keeps fading.** Survodutide's type-2-diabetes Phase 3 (1 October 2026) showed
8.2-9.8% weight loss counting all randomised patients and repeated the roughly one-in-five
gastrointestinal drop-out rate.

🔴 **A better-capitalised in-class rival is ahead.** Lilly's eloralintide shows roughly double the
weight loss at comparable tolerability on its lower doses, and started Phase 3 about a year earlier.

🔴 **Runway guidance still withdrawn** while the company carries 50% of a large Phase 3.

🔴 **No insider buying** (scan insider buy ratio 0.00) even at a 52-week low.

🟢 **Tolerability confirmed again** - 1.9% versus 1.7% gastrointestinal discontinuation (7 October
2026).

🟢 **Roche committed with all the data in hand** - a three-trial, roughly 7,000-participant Phase 3
programme started in October 2026. A partner that has seen both Phase 2 readouts and chooses to fund
half of a programme this size is a costly, informative signal.

🟢 **Capital returned, not diluted** - the DKK 1.3bn buyback completed early on 5 October 2026,
cutting shares outstanding to about 66.3m.

🟢 **Net cash of about DKK 199 a share against a DKK 233.80 price** - the market now values all the
operating assets at roughly DKK 35 a share, about DKK 2.3bn or USD 0.36bn.

---

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

**The product's role has shifted from "lose weight" to "keep it off."** Management's 2025 vocabulary
moved from magnitude to "a therapy that patients can and will accept to stay on." William Blair's 8
October 2026 note now says petrelintide will likely be used mainly in the maintenance setting. That is
a smaller market than first-line weight loss, but it is a real one, and it is exactly where a
placebo-like side-effect profile matters most.

**The combination is now the real bet.** The Phase 2 combination with Roche's enicepatide (planned for
the second half of 2026) and the revived GIP analog both point to a company whose upside sits in
amylin-based combinations rather than in petrelintide alone.

**The fall was not only company-specific.** The shares went from DKK 306 (7 September) to about DKK
266 (5 October) - a span that includes the 1 October survodutide data - and then to DKK 233.80 after
the 7 October readout. The whole obesity group de-rated in the same window: on 12 October Structure Therapeutics sits at its 52-week low (about 42% below its 50-day
average), Gubra about 16% below its 50-day average, Viking about 14% below, and Novo Nordisk near its
lows. Part of Zealand's fall is a sector-wide sell-off, not news about Zealand.

**Buying back stock at DKK 290-300 and then watching it fall to DKK 234** is a reminder that
management's capital-return timing was early. The buyback was value-accretive only if the base case
holds.

---

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: PIVOTING.** Zealand has turned from a broad, efficacy-led pipeline into a
concentrated, partner-funded, tolerability-led amylin franchise, and it is recycling capital - pausing
an asset, selling a royalty, buying back shares - rather than compounding an earnings base.

**The single thing to weigh before sizing.** At DKK 233.80 the market is paying about DKK 35 a share
above net cash for half of a Phase-3 amylin, a royalty on a Phase-3-positive survodutide, two
rare-disease assets and the platform. The cash is not a floor: it is earmarked to fund Zealand's half
of the Phase 3 programme into the late 2020s, and runway guidance has not been given since February
2025. The question is how much of the roughly DKK 13.2bn survives the development bill, and whether a
roughly 10%, very well-tolerated amylin earns a real share of a maintenance market that Lilly and Novo
will also contest. Size to that question, not to the enterprise value.

**Economic moat: NARROW, and eroding.** The moat is intangible - composition-of-matter patents,
long peptide know-how, and an integrated Roche alliance that would be costly to unwind. It is real but
narrowing: return on invested capital is negative (-24.9%), the 99.7% gross margin is milestone
accounting, and the one differentiator (tolerability) is matched at much higher efficacy by Lilly's
in-class molecule.

**Secular threat: manageable.** Obesity-drug net-price compression - cash-pay channels and payer
pressure - shrinks the pie every amylin will share, but the category is growing from a low
penetration base, so this dilutes rather than destroys terminal value. The bigger threat is
competitive, not secular.

**Fear-print or value trap?** Closer to a fear-print than at our last look. The October data were
modestly disappointing, not thesis-breaking, and much of the further fall coincided with a sector-wide
sell-off; the price now sits far nearer our adverse case than our central one. It is not a value trap
in the usual sense - there is no shrinking earnings base - but it remains an option on one molecule,
cushioned by cash that will be spent.

Management credibility 3 of 5 · trajectory turning · a narrow but real moat · moat trend eroding · structural threat manageable.
thesis_evidence: The thesis holds. Its load-bearing claims are each corroborated by dated facts: net cash covers most of the price (DKK 14,457m cash and securities against DKK 411m debt at 30 June 2026; buyback completed 5 October 2026, about 66.3m shares outstanding); the partner is committed (Roche and Zealand started a three-trial, roughly 7,000-participant Phase 3 on 7 October 2026 with both Phase 2 datasets in hand); and tolerability is real (1.9% versus 1.7% gastrointestinal discontinuation in ZUPREME-2, 7 October 2026, after 4.8% versus 4.9% in ZUPREME-1, 5 March 2026). The efficacy shortfall was already known at our last look and is now priced into a lower fair value rather than treated as a broken thesis. The fall from DKK 306.30 (7 September) to DKK 233.80 (12 October 2026) came from company news - the survodutide diabetes Phase 3 on 1 October (shares down more than 8%) and the petrelintide diabetes readout on 7 October (down 3-4% on 8 October) - on top of a sector-wide sell-off in obesity names over the same weeks, not from forced selling.
macro_fit_note: The backdrop is reflation (growth up, inflation hot at 3.35% CPI through August 2026) in a debt-cycle phase of discipline, where positive real long rates punish long-duration stories and reward cash flow; Zealand is the opposite profile - negative free cash flow with value resting on drugs launching late in the decade - so the macro is a headwind, softened only by net cash covering most of the price. Its inflation-resilience label reads exposed, but that rests on milestone-driven swings in gross margin rather than pricing power; there is no pass-through evidence in the transcript, as the company has no product sales of its own.

bull_thesis:
The bull case is now mostly arithmetic. At DKK 233.80 (Copenhagen, 12 October 2026) Zealand's market value is about DKK 15.5bn on roughly 66.3m shares outstanding after the buyback completed on 5 October 2026. Against that sits net cash of about DKK 13.2bn - DKK 14,457m of cash and securities less DKK 411m of debt at 30 June 2026, less the roughly DKK 0.9bn of buyback spent after June, with the USD 100m Royalty Pharma payment of August 2026 broadly offsetting third-quarter spending. That is about DKK 199 a share, or roughly 85% of the share price. The market is paying about DKK 35 a share - an enterprise value (market value less net cash) of about DKK 2.3bn, or roughly USD 0.36bn - for everything Zealand owns.

On 7 October 2026, with both Phase 2 datasets in hand, Roche committed to a three-trial Phase 3 programme of about 7,000 participants for petrelintide - in people with obesity, people with type 2 diabetes, and people with cardiovascular disease. A partner that has already paid a large upfront does not fund half of the most expensive kind of trial programme in medicine on a molecule it doubts. Zealand owns half of the United States and European profit, plus royalties elsewhere, with Roche carrying all commercial manufacturing.

The October diabetes data also corroborate a narrower claim management made in February 2025: that amylin may work about as well in people with diabetes as without, which GLP-1 drugs do not. A 9.2% weight loss at only 28 weeks in diabetes sits close to the 10.7% seen at 42 weeks in people without diabetes. And tolerability held a second time - 1.9% gastrointestinal discontinuation against 1.7% on placebo. In a market where most patients stop GLP-1 drugs within a year, a drug people can stay on has a real home in maintenance - keeping weight off after an initial loss - which is how William Blair now frames it (8 October 2026). Conditions: the development bill stays near DKK 5-6bn net of milestones, Phase 3 confirms the tolerability profile at scale, and the maintenance market proves sizeable.
bear_thesis:
The bear case is that the cash is not a floor and the molecule keeps disappointing. Three readouts in seven months have each been 'positive but not enough': 10.7% weight loss at 42 weeks (5 March 2026) against a 15-20% target management repeated across five calls; survodutide's type-2-diabetes Phase 3 (1 October 2026) at 8.2-9.8% counting all randomised patients with about one in five stopping for gastrointestinal side effects; and petrelintide in diabetes (7 October 2026) at 9.2% with an HbA1c fall of only up to 0.65 points, which William Blair called underwhelming. bull_thesis:
The bull case is now mostly arithmetic. At DKK 233.80 (Copenhagen, 12 October 2026) Zealand's market value is about DKK 15.5bn on roughly 66.3m shares outstanding after the buyback completed on 5 October 2026. Against that sits net cash of about DKK 13.2bn - DKK 14,457m of cash and securities less DKK 411m of debt at 30 June 2026, less the roughly DKK 0.9bn of buyback spent after June, with the USD 100m Royalty Pharma payment of August 2026 broadly offsetting third-quarter spending. That is about DKK 199 a share, or roughly 85% of the share price. The market is paying about DKK 35 a share - an enterprise value (market value less net cash) of about DKK 2.3bn, or roughly USD 0.36bn - for everything Zealand owns.

What that buys has just been re-validated by the people with the most information. On 7 October 2026, with both Phase 2 datasets in hand, Roche committed to a three-trial Phase 3 programme of about 7,000 participants for petrelintide - in people with obesity, people with type 2 diabetes, and people with cardiovascular disease. A partner that has already paid a large upfront does not fund half of the most expensive kind of trial programme in medicine on a molecule it doubts. Zealand owns half of the United States and European profit, plus royalties elsewhere, with Roche carrying all commercial manufacturing.

The October diabetes data also corroborate a narrower claim management made in February 2025: that amylin may work about as well in people with diabetes as without, which GLP-1 drugs do not. A 9.2% weight loss at only 28 weeks in diabetes sits close to the 10.7% seen at 42 weeks in people without diabetes. And tolerability held a second time - 1.9% gastrointestinal discontinuation against 1.7% on placebo. In a market where most patients stop GLP-1 drugs within a year, a drug people can stay on has a real home in maintenance - keeping weight off after an initial loss - which is how William Blair now frames it (8 October 2026). Add the royalty on Boehringer's survodutide, now positive in two Phase 3 trials with the liver-disease programme still to come, two rare-disease assets (glepaglutide for short bowel syndrome in European review, dasiglucagon for congenital hyperinsulinism), a combination trial with Roche's enicepatide planned for the second half of 2026, and an early pipeline.

Finally, much of the latest fall is a sector-wide sell-off rather than Zealand-specific news: on 12 October 2026 Structure Therapeutics is at its 52-week low, about 42% below its 50-day average; Gubra is about 16% below; Viking about 14% below. When the whole obesity group de-rates, a name whose price is 85% cash is the one most likely to be mispriced. Conditions: the development bill stays near DKK 5-6bn net of milestones, Phase 3 confirms the tolerability profile at scale, and the maintenance market proves sizeable.
bear_thesis:
The bear case is that the cash is not a floor and the molecule keeps disappointing. Three readouts in seven months have each been 'positive but not enough': 10.7% weight loss at 42 weeks (5 March 2026) against a 15-20% target management repeated across five calls; survodutide's type-2-diabetes Phase 3 (1 October 2026) at 8.2-9.8% counting all randomised patients with about one in five stopping for gastrointestinal side effects; and petrelintide in diabetes (7 October 2026) at 9.2% with an HbA1c fall of only up to 0.65 points, which William Blair called underwhelming. The market sold each one.

The competitive problem is not new but it is getting sharper. Eli Lilly's eloralintide, an amylin of the same class, reported Phase 2 weight loss of up to about 20% at 48 weeks in November 2025 with tolerability similar to placebo at its lower doses, and entered Phase 3 around the end of 2025 - roughly a year ahead of petrelintide, including a diabetes trial. Novo Nordisk's cagrilintide, inside CagriSema, is further ahead still. Petrelintide's one differentiator, tolerability, is matched by a rival with about double the efficacy and a trillion-dollar balance sheet. A 'maintenance' positioning is a smaller and more price-sensitive market than first-line weight loss, and obesity net prices are already compressing.

Meanwhile the cash is committed. The trailing-twelve-month free cash flow to 30 June 2026 is negative DKK 1.80bn; consensus forward earnings growth is about -66%; return on invested capital is -24.9%; the Piotroski financial-strength score is 3 of 9. Full-year 2026 revenue guidance was booked in the first half, so the second half and 2027 carry costs with little revenue. Zealand now pays half of a roughly 7,000-participant Phase 3 programme, a Boston build-out and its own rare-disease work, and has given no cash-runway guidance since February 2025. If net spending reaches DKK 8bn before petrelintide earns anything, about half of the roughly DKK 16.45bn of net cash and receivables is gone - leaving about DKK 127 a share of cash - and the operating assets are worth little; even then the adverse case is about DKK 190 a share, roughly 19% below today's price. The screener's 2.6x price-to-free-cash-flow multiple and DKK 522.8 discounted-cash-flow value are milestone artifacts and should be ignored. What would confirm the bear: a larger-than-expected development bill in the third-quarter report or 2027 guidance, a weak combination signal, or further rival amylin data widening the efficacy gap.
consensus_delta: Where we disagree with the market is now mostly about the cash, not the science. On the science we agree with the street: petrelintide is a very well-tolerated, roughly 10% weight-loss amylin, not the 15-20% best-in-class drug management promised, and William Blair's 8 October 2026 note - weight loss 'intriguing', blood sugar underwhelming, few meaningful catalysts within a year, likely used mainly for maintenance - is fair. One reported price-target cut, from DKK 400 to DKK 300 on lower peak-sales assumptions for petrelintide and survodutide, points the same way; we could not pin its exact date, and FMP has no target coverage for this listing. Where we disagree: at DKK 233.80 the market is paying about DKK 35 a share above net cash - roughly USD 0.36bn of enterprise value - for half of a drug Roche has just committed to a 7,000-participant Phase 3, a royalty on a twice-Phase-3-positive survodutide, two rare-disease assets and a platform. Even after charging a DKK 5.5bn development bill, our base case values those parts at about DKK 7bn net, against DKK 2.3bn priced. The market is either assuming a development bill near our adverse DKK 8bn with little to show for it, or it is selling the whole obesity group and not distinguishing a name that is 85% cash. We also disagree with our own screener: the 2.6x price-to-free-cash-flow multiple, the 70% net margin and the DKK 522.8 discounted-cash-flow value are all the 2025 Roche upfront payment and say nothing about value.
forcing_function: There is no fixed-date, contractual event that forces a re-rating. The re-rating, if it comes, is the market recognising that it is paying almost nothing above cash for partner-funded late-stage assets. Near-term markers, none with a fixed date or payout: the third-quarter report (expected mid-November 2026), which should give the first post-Phase-3-start view of spending; the start of the Phase 2 combination with Roche's enicepatide (guided to the second half of 2026); Boehringer's survodutide liver-disease and cardiovascular-outcome data; and regulatory steps on glepaglutide in Europe and dasiglucagon in the United States. The decisive data - petrelintide Phase 3 - are years away. This is a valuation case, not an event case, and we size it as one.
valley_of_death: The next three to nine months hold more ways to disappoint than to delight, but no way to break the company. The third-quarter report (expected mid-November 2026) will show a loss: full-year collaboration revenue guidance of DKK 4.5bn was booked in the first half, so the second half carries operating cost against almost no revenue. That is arithmetic, not deterioration, but headline sellers may not distinguish. More important is any first word on 2027 spending and Zealand's share of the Phase 3 bill - with runway guidance withdrawn since February 2025, a figure above our DKK 5.5bn base would push value toward the adverse case. There is no liquidity risk: total debt is DKK 411m against roughly DKK 13bn of cash and securities, and the solvency score in our scan is 7.5. There is no debt wall, no dividend to cut and no covenant. The risks are scientific and competitive: further amylin data from Lilly or Novo widening the efficacy gap, an early signal from the enicepatide combination that disappoints, or continued de-rating of the obesity group in a reflation backdrop that punishes long-dated cash flows. With the buyback finished on 5 October 2026, the company is no longer a buyer of its own shares.
positioning_washout: Most of the forced-selling pressure appears spent. Zealand's register is growth and specialist-biotech money, not yield or index money, so there is no dividend-cut or index-deletion mechanism to force further sales. Holders have now absorbed four disappointing prints in seven months - March, June, 1 October and 7 October 2026 - and the price sits at its 52-week low, about 21% below its 50-day average of DKK 295 and 28% below its 200-day average of DKK 323. Two cautions. First, the buyback that supported the shares since May 2026 completed on 5 October 2026, removing a steady buyer. Second, the latest leg coincided with a sector-wide sell-off across obesity names (Structure, Gubra, Viking), which can persist independently of Zealand's own news. We do not see mechanical, value-blind selling that would be worth waiting for.
moderator_conclusion:
Buy now.

At our last look on 7 September 2026, at DKK 306.30, Zealand was a reasonable business at about a fair price, and we chose to wait for a better one. The better price has arrived - DKK 233.80 on 12 October 2026, about 24% lower - but it came with news, so we lowered our fair value before deciding. Two readouts in the first week of October were each positive but underwhelming: Boehringer's survodutide in type 2 diabetes (1 October), with about one in five patients stopping for stomach side effects, and petrelintide in type 2 diabetes (7 October), with 9.2% weight loss at 28 weeks and a modest blood-sugar effect. We cut our base value for petrelintide and survodutide and raised the development bill, taking fair value from DKK 348 to DKK 305 a share.

Even at the lower value the shares now sit about 23% below it, clearing the 20% discount we require in today's reflation backdrop. The case is simple: net cash of roughly DKK 199 a share covers about 85% of the price, so the market pays about DKK 35 a share - roughly USD 0.36bn - for half of a drug Roche has just committed to a 7,000-participant Phase 3, a royalty on a twice-Phase-3-positive survodutide, two rare-disease assets and a platform. The thesis holds: the cash, the partner commitment and the tolerability are all confirmed by dated facts.

Be clear about what this is. It is an option on one molecule, cushioned by cash that will be spent - not a cash-backed floor. The payoff now leans our way: about DKK 71 up to fair value against about DKK 44 down to our adverse case of DKK 190, roughly 1.6 to 1, with further skew to the favorable case of DKK 565. That adverse case was raised from DKK 142 once it counted the roughly DKK 3.8bn of Roche milestone receivables on the 30 June 2026 balance sheet and the first rusfertide payment - even after a DKK 8bn development bill, about DKK 127 a share of cash remains. The moat is narrow and eroding - Lilly's eloralintide matches petrelintide's tolerability with roughly twice the weight loss and a year's head start - and the macro backdrop, which rewards cash flow now, is a headwind for a company with none. Part of the latest fall is a sector-wide sell-off in obesity names rather than Zealand news. Our conviction stays at a middling 3: the business is no better than in September, only cheaper. Size it as a modest position, and watch the third-quarter report in mid-November for the first read on Zealand's share of the Phase 3 bill - a figure well above DKK 5.5bn net would move us toward the adverse case.
